#412. Big-ticket holiday items may be harder to find as shipping costs rise

This holiday season, big-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs. All of that is forcing many retailers to rethink their holiday inventory strategy.

"We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these big-ticket items we have seen in history," said Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.

Weinswig said retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of big-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.

"It's freight getting it from there to here; it's carrying costs; then it's just the trucking to get it into the stores," Weinswig said. "We're talking three different pieces right here and each is up significantly year on year."

The surge pricing for supply chain services is being caused by domestic and international policy.

According to Evercore ISI, the rates for general trucking have increased more than 47% year over year during the week of Nov. 2.

Industry experts say a large factor has been a crackdown by the federal government on non-citizen truck drivers and non-U.S.-based truck drivers operating in the U.S. That has created a capacity crunch that has raised rates and is expected to continue to create upward pressure.

At the same time, fuel surcharges are spiking.

Most transportation providers charge customers an extra fuel surcharge to offset changes in the cost of diesel fuel. That surcharge has spiked 64% year over year, according to Evercore ISI data, as diesel prices have hit new record highs due in part to the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.

And inventory holding costs — or the total expense of storing unsold goods, which could include the costs for capital, service, storage and other risk factors — are closely tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which exceeded 5% in October and remains at multiyear highs in November.

Collectively, the higher costs could mean bigger discounts for shoppers willing to wait, according to Bill Catania, CEO of logistics technology company OneRail, which powers same-day delivery for companies such as FedEx and Lowe's.

"You're going to see more discount and price promotions as we get closer to the holiday to liquidate inventory, so they're not having to transfer it or dispose of it or position it some other way," Catania said.

Retailers are also facing a conundrum in their holiday inventory strategy when it comes to shipping costs versus opportunity costs. In other words, is it worth it to stock up now, or wait it out in hopes that shipping rates will come down some but potentially miss out on having the right product mix?

It's leading to a wait-and-see approach for stocking shelves after early holiday sales in October, executives said.

UPS CEO Carol Tomé said on the company's earnings call on Oct. 27 that it's "just starting to get peak season forecasts from our customers."

Similarly, Derek Leathers, CEO of Werner Enterprises, a trucker for big-box stores and major retailers, said retailers are cautious.

"When rates are higher and the cost of capital is more expensive, you are going to have a much more intense focus on not having excess inventory," Leathers said.

Still, 2026 holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion as inflation drives growth and customer spending is expected to remain healthy, according to Bain & Company's annual forecast. Leathers said even with the surge in trucking and shipping rates, he's seeing that retailers are willing to pay up to stock up.

"The bigger concern right now is wanting to make sure they have their capacity locked in. There is way more dialogue around the assurance of having a truck or whatever mode that needs to be secured," Leathers said. "Not saying they are price insensitive, because they are certainly always concerned about price. But you can't sell it if it's not on the shelf."

ShipMatrix, a data analytics firm for the logistics industry, forecasts 2.4 billion packages will be delivered during the 2026 holiday peak, a 4% increase year over year.

It's an increase that will likely lead retailers to increasingly use gig delivery, especially later in the holiday peak. Gig workers allow retailers and delivery companies to adjust to changes in order flow and accommodate surges of last-minute shopping without spending time and money onboarding new team members.

"Gig economy delivery is great. You know, it fulfills fast, but there's better unit economics out there," Catania said.

Industry experts said they also expect to see more retailers use drones for last-mile delivery for smaller items.

A 2024 PwC study forecast that the cost of drone delivery would "drop by more than 70% over the next 10 years, which will not only match traditional last-mile delivery costs, but surpass them and create an inflection point for the industry."

Amit Regev, CEO of drone company Flytrex, said the company is in active talks with retailers about using drones for holiday deliveries.

"The expectation now is becoming so much more instant," Regev said.

Retailers have been increasing their use of drones. Lowe's in September said it was launching a drone delivery service in partnership with DoorDash and Alphabet's Wing. Amazon earlier this year said it was aiming to offer drone deliveries in nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year.

Flytrex currently delivers for Walmart and a number of restaurants including Little Caesars and Papa John's.

"Customers are looking for that instant gratification," Regev said. "So if it takes too long, they might not want to order with you. And from what we are seeing that's a stronger incentive for them to try and test or deploy deliveries using drones."

#411. Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers (2026): Anker, ESR, Satechi

A three-in-one travel charger that can power up my iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods is one of the first items I pack for any trip. I’ve tried out plenty of options, but these are my favorite chargers for keeping the holy trinity of Apple gadgets going strong while on vacation or a work trip.

Many of these picks will also happily charge Qi2 Android phones and other devices that support wireless charging. Since space is at a premium when traveling, they all feature clever compact designs. I’ve also included two-in-one options if you want to travel even lighter.

If you want something for your desk or nightstand when you’re back home, check out our Best Apple 3-in-1 Wireless Charging Stations and Best Wireless Chargers guides, and for power on the go, read our Best Travel Adapters, Best Power Banks, and Best MagSafe Power Banks guides.

Updated November 2026: I added chargers from Peak Design and Mophie, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.

A classy look elevates this folding three-in-one stand charger, which accommodates your phone in portrait or landscape orientation. It is Qi2 25W-certified, so it can deliver 25 watts to supported phones (15 watts to others). There’s a fold-out Apple Watch charger on the back to fast-charge Apple Watch (Series 7 and above), and a spot for earbuds on the base. It feels sturdy and secure, with rubber grips to prevent sliding, and supports StandBy mode. It’s relatively compact for travel, but also looks good enough to be your permanent bedside charger. Not only does the whole thing fold flat, but it also comes with UK and EU adapters for the included power brick.

Satechi’s latest model is plastic with a soft-touch finish; the original version ($130) was more luxurious, with vegan leather and aluminum. The original is still a great option if you don’t mind the 15-watt charging rate.

Packing space is often limited when you travel, so it’s very handy that Anker’s MagGo folds down to a slim, compact form. Despite the small size, it packs plenty of power, charging your iPhone or Qi2-certified phone at up to 15 watts on a magnetic pad that you can adjust to your preferred angle. A second pad behind the main one charges AirPods or other wireless earbuds, and there’s a fold-out Apple Watch charger.

It can feel a little crowded when fully loaded, but I appreciate the space-saving design when packing it in a bag. While you can find faster options with chargers that support Qi2 25W, they’re not widely available and make little difference if you charge your devices overnight.

This cute, compact charging kit comes in a soft faux-leather bag. Unzip it to find a folding charger with a tiltable pad for your iPhone, a pad underneath for your AirPods, and a pop-up Apple Watch charger to the side. It comes with a 5-foot USB-C cable and a power adapter with fold-out prongs and three plug attachments (EU, UK, and AU). Everything is color-matched in black or cream, unless you opt for the special edition in orange and teal.

ESR’s folding charger delivers 25-watt charging for Qi2 25W-supported phones, fast Apple Watch charging, and an effective cooling fan. This three-in-one model folds away neatly and has a strong magnetic pad that supports portrait or landscape orientation. You can also adjust the angles for the phone and watch chargers. The fan is relatively quiet, but I prefer total silence at night, so I was pleased to find a button that turns it off for when you’re trying to sleep.

The plastic construction doesn’t feel premium, but it is lightweight, and the rubber feet do a decent job of preventing it from sliding around. It is more expensive than ESR’s previous release, the HaloLock, and the faster charging probably isn’t worth it if you’re primarily charging overnight, but overall it is a decent travel charger with a speed boost.

With a clean white finish, an elegant folding design, and warm ambient light, this Journey charger is a delightful travel companion. Ordinarily, I hate superfluous lights on a charger, but this isn’t a pointless LED; it’s a gentle glow from behind the Apple Watch shelf on the back, with a touch-sensitive power button on the front. It’s nice to have when you wake up in an unfamiliar, pitch-dark hotel room. You can fold it out to stand mode to charge all three Apple gadgets at once, or lay it flat if you just need to charge your iPhone and AirPods.

While this folding charger isn’t quite as compact as Anker’s below, I love that you can use the iPhone charging pad when it’s folded up. The Apple Watch charger can also pop up for Nightstand mode. It’s finished in a soft faux leather and folds flat for easy carrying in the included pouch. You get a cable to plug into the USB-C port, but no power supply, so you’ll need to provide a 30-watt power adapter. There is also a two-in-one version ($80) for just your iPhone and Apple Watch.

If you are really pressed for space, this is the smallest three-in-one charger you can get. It folds up to resemble a macaron and is easy to stow, but it’s not a power bank, so you do still need a cable and wall charger (both supplied). Unfolded, you get a magnetic pad to charge your iPhone at up to 15 watts, a middle pad for your AirPods, and an Apple Watch charger on the right. The design is lovely to handle, with a soft-touch finish and a durable silicone strap. I still prefer stand-style chargers because they allow you to angle your iPhone and use StandBy mode, but the MagGo UFO lets you travel as light as possible.

More stylish and compact than the other options listed here, this two-in-one charger from Peak Design folds flat for easy stowing. Open it to reveal a base with a channel for a USB-C cable and a Qi2 25W charging pad, plus a second swiveling Qi2 25W pad on top. You can charge two phones, or a phone and wireless earbuds. There’s also a USB-C port on the side, so you can plug in a third device, or a watch or ring charger. It comes with a cable, but you’ll need a power adapter (45-watt minimum). I like Peak Design’s 65W Dual Slim Charger ($65), but you don’t have to spend that much.

This genius petite gadget is perfect for folks who love to travel light. It’s an Apple Watch charger with a handy carabiner you can clip to your key ring or bag strap. Rotate the magnetic pad, and a USB-C jack pops out. Just to be clear, this is not a power bank—you must plug it into your MacBook, a USB-C port on a wall adapter, or even your iPhone to charge your Apple Watch. It doesn’t get more portable than this.

UAG SRGE 3-in-1 Travel and Desktop Charger for $100: This charger was close to earning a top spot until I saw the price (regularly $165). It’s a very smart charging kit that folds flat and comes in a snazzy zip-up bag with a 4-foot braided USB-C cable and a 25-watt power adapter, including plugs for the US, UK, and Europe. You can prop your iPhone at different angles on the MagSafe stand, and it works well with StandBy mode and Nightstand mode for your Apple Watch, but it’s not Qi2-certified, so you won’t get the stated 15-watt charging for an iPhone.

Mophie 3-in-1 Travel Charger With MagSafe for $150: This little travel kit is the older version of our pick above, but it’s still good (especially if you find it on sale). It also comes with a carrying case, charging brick, and USB-C cable. The square stack unfolds to reveal three wireless chargers in one elongated pad. The iPhone sticks magnetically to the center (15 watts), and the Apple Watch dock supports Nightstand mode. There’s also a grooved spot for the AirPods. It works well and is pretty lightweight and compact.

Twelve South Butterfly Travel 2-in-1 MagSafe Charger for $80: This uber-compact two-in-one charger looks like a hockey puck. Open the Butterfly, and you’ll find two pads attached with a rubbery silicone material. You can fast-charge an Apple Watch on one—even popping the charger up to take advantage of Nightstand mode—and the other circle lets you recharge your MagSafe iPhone at 15 watts. It’s a super compact solution, and Twelve South includes a 30-watt power source and cable with international plug adapters.

Native Union Voyage 2-in-1 MagSafe Charger for $100: For a slightly lower price, former WIRED reviews editor Adrienne So likes Native Union’s Qi2 butterfly solution, which doesn’t include plug adapters but comes in a tidy travel pouch and includes a cable.

Kuxiu Qi2 25W Travel Charging Station: This charger folds down to an impressively small package, and it feels sturdy with a silicone-covered metal construction. It can hit 25 watts for supported Qi2 25W phones, comes in a few different finishes, and ships with a 45-watt power adapter and USB-C cable in the box. Unfortunately, I don’t like how it looks, and I found it awkward to charge all three devices at once. It’s actually so compact that it feels crowded.

Mous Travel Charger: While the compact, folding design and low price impressed me, it gets kinda warm when you charge all three of your Apple devices, and the AirPods spot is finicky.

Most of my picks are MagSafe or Qi2-certified wireless chargers. That means they take advantage of the magnets embedded in the back of the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, iPhone 17, and iPhone 18 ranges. The magnets ensure perfect alignment, enabling faster and more efficient wireless charging.

Qi2 is a wireless charging standard that Apple worked with the Wireless Power Consortium to develop. Compared to the original Qi standard, it brings MagSafe-style magnetic charging, enabling faster charging rates and improved efficiency. Apple updated the iPhone 12 and newer to support Qi2, but it’s not just for Apple phones; other phones can get Qi2 certification. While Qi2 Android phones are still thin on the ground, you’ll find Qi2 in Google's Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series, and there are Qi2-ready phones that add magnets via a compatible case.

Qi2 charging mostly goes up to 15 watts, but the Qi2.2 update, branded as Qi2 25W, goes up to 25 watts. Support for Qi2 25W is currently limited and includes the iPhone 17 and 18 range and the Pixel 10 Pro XL and Pixel 11 range.

If you use a case, make sure it is MagSafe- or Qi2-compatible. A normal case will weaken the pull of the magnets in the device and will not stick to chargers as well. If your case is too thick, your phone may not charge at all.

MagSafe is also available in the AirPods charging case (depending on your model). Apple’s AirPods and AirPods Pro with the wireless charging case work with nearly all standard Qi wireless charging pads (as do many third-party wireless earbuds), but if you have AirPods with MagSafe, you can also connect them to magnetic mounts.

I mention StandBy and Nightstand modes throughout this guide, but what are they?

StandBy mode was introduced in iOS 17. When you place your iPhone on a charger in landscape orientation, it turns the screen into a smart display to show the time (with different clock designs to choose from), photos from your library, or widgets. If your iPhone supports an always-on screen, you can set it to turn off automatically after a set time when the iPhone isn't in use or when the room is dark. Head to Settings > Standby to customize it.

Nightstand mode shows the time on your Apple Watch when it’s sitting upright and charging, so it can serve as a bedside clock. You can customize this on your Apple Watch by heading to Settings > General > Nightstand mode.

#408. Novo says Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial

Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.

Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial.

When evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.

The detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications.

"This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," said Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity.

In 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040.

While Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6.

In Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.

But more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September.

"We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina said.

Novo said Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The company added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids.

Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said.

"That is something that is still an evidence gap," she said, pointing to the potential of future research.

#406. Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess

Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

But just as he’s leaving, the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

“Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Already, competitors have started to move in.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.

And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.

Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.

Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.

But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.

But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.

Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.

“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

#405. 'We slept here': Flight delays linger as airlines recover from ground stop, but schedule improves Monday

U.S. flights delays eased on Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on track after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday.

Nearly 300 U.S. flights were canceled and close to 1,000 were delayed Monday, a fraction of Sunday's disruptions, according to FlightAware data.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the weekend tied the issue that prompted officials to call for the ground stop to a router in southern Arkansas and work to update copper wires to a fiber-optic system overseen by L3Harris Technologies. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over to fiber optic.

Officials ordered the ground stop before 4 p.m. ET on Friday and it lasted until after 8 p.m. ET, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded and about 18,000 U.S. flights were canceled from Friday through Monday morning, according to FlightAware.

Over that period, American Airlines had the most cancellations with 5,367 flights, close to 22% of its schedule, followed by Delta Air Lines with 3,434 cancellations, or 17% of its schedule, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Southwest Airlines and United Airlines each canceled more than 16% of their schedules. Bad weather on Thursday and Friday had also contributed to disruptions before the ground stop.

On Sunday, disruptions lingered but were starting to improve.

"We slept here," said Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from New York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter's birthday trip. The two were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta, they decided to make good use of the extra time: After strolling through Central Park, they went window shopping on Fifth Avenue.

But when the flight was canceled, the standby list for a backup flight looked grim and their original midtown hotel was charging about $700 for an additional night, the two slept at LaGuardia on Saturday. She said they found wheelchairs to sleep in outside security.

Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays.

Customers told CNBC they were booked on several flights before getting on board.

Justine Fritz, who works in sales for a consumer goods company, was in New York for a business event on Friday. She tried five different flights before getting on one to Houston, then flew four hours out of her way to get back to Minneapolis after her Saturday flight was canceled. Fritz said she had so many boarding passes that the Transportation Security Administration wouldn't let her through security at first.

"It's been bananas," she told CNBC at the gate. Fritz said she made the best of it by shopping and getting a haircut, but she's still disappointed.

"I'm missing the first hour of the Vikings game," she said.

Martin said her trip home with her daughter will take even longer. Delta booked them to Memphis, and her husband will drive the four hours from Birmingham to pick them up.

Officials are investigating the root cause that led to what the FAA described as "instability" in data feeds. Duffy said Sunday that two routers, the original one detected as a problem in southern Arkansas, and another in Amarillo, Texas, are in an L3Harris lab in Florida.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday afternoon.

President Donald Trump said Monday he didn't "take any responsibility" for the ground stop.

Shortly after the ground stop, Duffy said he was asking Congress for as much as $50 billion for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system. A day later, Democratic lawmakers pushed back, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

"Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again," said Reps. Rick Larsen, D.-Wash., ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Andre Carson, D.-Ind., ranking member of the aviation subcommittee, in a joint statement.

#402. Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond

Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise.

Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

Pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic.

The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve said. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."

In 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios, which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion. Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't announced a projected release date.

#401. The full GTA 6 soundtrack reportedly leaked: See every artist and track

What's a Grand Theft Auto game without a killer soundtrack?

From the sun-soaked synth-pop of Vice City to surfing a sea of radio stations, music has always been an essential part of Rockstar Games' gritty, open-world franchise. And with Grand Theft Auto VI taking players back to Vice City, the sprawling soundtrack is shaping up to be just as ambitious as the game itself.

Rockstar has already revealed a 34-track album featuring artists like Travis Scott, Cardi B, and PinkPantheress, along with an original score composed by the French electronic duo Justice. Meanwhile, the game's fictional radio stations are bringing some familiar voices to the airwaves, including Robyn, Bad Bunny, and Lana Del Rey.

And that's just what we know so far. Ahead of GTA 6's Nov. 19 release, we're keeping track of every confirmed song, artist, radio station, and celebrity DJ coming to Leonida. Consider this your unofficial guide to the sounds of Vice City.

Rockstar has announced Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, a 34-track collection of original music arriving Nov. 19, the same day as the game.

The album features an eclectic mix of artists and genres, from hip-hop heavyweights Travis Scott and Cardi B to country star Morgan Wallen and Puerto Rican singer Rauw Alejandro. There's even a collaboration between CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, PinkPantheress, Fred again.., and French producer Etienne de Crécy. And somehow, someway, Morgan Wallen's single is the most-streamed track from the soundtrack on Spotify, with more than 25 million streams. Yung Lean, fight back!

On Nov. 14, Billboard confirmed the full tracklist:

"Starting From Zero" — Justice feat. Michael McDonald

"That's It" — Yung Lean feat. Future & Metro Boomin

"Sexy Magic" — CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, PinkPantheress, Fred again.. & Étienne de Crécy

"Flower in a Hurricane" — Justice feat. Tame Impala, SZA & King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard

"Dance With Me" — A Boogie Wit Da Hoodie feat. Elkan

"Bright Lights, Big City" — Keith Richards

"Stone Kold Krazy Luuv" — Jesse Johnson & Dâm-Funk

"Overtown Lights" — Stanley Clarke, Yussef Dayes & Robert Glasper

Fans can listen to the available singles on Rockstar's official GTA 6 music website, where the album is also available to pre-save or pre-order on vinyl and CD.

The French electronic duo Justice, consisting of Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay, is responsible for the original score of Grand Theft Auto VI.

Rockstar confirmed the news on Oct. 15 alongside the game's launch trailer, which features the debut of Justice's new single, "Flower in a Hurricane," featuring Tame Impala, SZA, and Australian psychedelic rock band King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard.

It's a fitting collaboration for a game returning to Vice City, a fictional playground known for its vibrant nightlife and electronic music. Justice's signature blend of distorted synths, disco, and dance music feels particularly suited to Rockstar's radiant criminal underworld.

The duo previously collaborated with Tame Impala on "Neverender" from their 2024 album Hyperdrama. The song won Best Dance/Electronic Recording at the 2025 Grammys.

Rockstar has also confirmed that an official score album is on the way, although additional details, including its release date and tracklist, have yet to be announced.

The fictional radio stations are one of Grand Theft Auto's most beloved features, and GTA 6 is bringing some major star power to the airwaves.

On Oct. 8, Rockstar unveiled six radio stations, each with its own musical identity and celebrity hosts. Among the biggest names are Bad Bunny, Robyn, Lana Del Rey, Burna Boy, and members of Slayer.

Here's a breakdown of the confirmed stations and their hosts:

Bad Bunny is bringing the sounds of Puerto Rico to Vice City. Alongside singer RaiNao, the superstar hosts Cocoteo FM, a station dedicated to modern Latin music, including reggaeton and other Caribbean sounds.

A familiar name for longtime Vice City fans, Flash FM returns with Swedish pop icon Robyn and model Alex Consani behind the microphone. The station promises a steady stream of pop music and dance-floor favorites.

Country music gets its own corner of Leonida with Back Country Radio, hosted by Morgan Wallen and Lana Del Rey. In perhaps the most unexpected casting choice, Del Rey's husband, Jeremy Dufrene, also makes an appearance as the station's "roving reporter, swamp meteorologist, and airboat captain."

Afrobeats superstar Burna Boy teams up with DJ and producer Palms Trax for a station spotlighting amapiano, African classics, and other sounds from across the continent.

Metal fans aren't being left out. Slayer's Kerry King and Tom Araya host The Chamber, a station dedicated to heavy metal.

Miami rap legends Trick Daddy and Trina are taking listeners through the history of Southern hip-hop on Dirty South Classics, a particularly fitting addition to a game inspired by South Florida.

These are only the stations Rockstar has revealed so far. The developer says GTA 6 will feature its biggest and most wide-ranging collection of in-game radio stations and podcasts yet, with everything from classic rock to talk radio.

Long before Rockstar began revealing the official soundtrack, the game's trailers were already giving fans a taste of what to expect musically.

The first GTA 6 trailer, released in December 2023, featured Tom Petty's "Love Is a Long Road," a track from his 1989 album Full Moon Fever. The song was an especially fitting choice given Petty's Florida roots and the game's focus on Jason and Lucia's relationship.

The Oct. 15, 2026, launch trailer introduced "Flower in a Hurricane," the new Justice collaboration featuring Tame Impala, SZA, and King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard.

Rockstar has launched an official music hub where fans can preview the game's radio stations and listen to singles from Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album.

The album arrives Nov. 19, 2026, alongside the game, with digital, vinyl, and CD editions planned.

As Rockstar reveals more music, we'll update this guide with additional songs, artists, radio stations, and soundtrack details.

#399. The Best Smart Bird Feeders for Backyard Birding (2026)

You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one. The best smart bird feeders are easily recognizable with their clear housing, cameras, and solar panels. Perhaps a friend or family member has sent you a photo or video of a bright goldfinch or a handsome woodpecker (guilty). But are these feeders really worth their $100-plus price tag? Are they durable? And what about the squirrel problem?

To answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints. I’ve explored the apps and notification settings, examined the photo and video quality, noted which features are hidden behind a subscription paywall, and used Cornell Lab’s All About Birds—as well as Google Lens and my own expertise—to verify the accuracy of AI identifications. The recommendations below are what I would buy with my own money, having tested dozens of brands and models for a minimum of four weeks each.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a new Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID. I've also removed a couple of discontinued feeders and updated links and prices.

This cheery blue- or yellow-roofed feeder, from security company Netvue, was the first smart feeder WIRED tested, back in 2022, when it earned a 6/10 rating due to its high price and wonky AI. Both metrics have improved dramatically since then—Birdfy's app is now the second-most user-friendly on the market, behind only Birdbuddy's, and this feeder is often on sale for around $130. Its AI identification, which is decent, used to be paywalled but is now free with every tier of feeder.

The 1080p/2K camera isn't the best quality you'll find, but it does have one of the widest viewing angles of any smart feeder, at 155 degrees, so you're more likely to get full bird shots, as opposed to just heads and butts. The plastic housing (available in blue or yellow) also makes this feeder durable and easy to clean, and the 50-ounce seed reservoir is super easy to fill with its convenient flip-up top. Not all bundles come with a solar panel, but you can buy one separately. Unlike with other feeders, the solar panel is not built in and needs to be mounted and connected separately with the included 9.8-foot charging cable.

It's not the fanciest feeder on the market, nor the one with the best camera, but I've never had a problem with the two models I've been rotating in and out throughout the years, and the reliability and price point make it the best bet for most backyard birders.

Birdbuddy's brand-new Nook model is a lot of bird feeder for the price; it won our recent head-to-head test of sub-$100 smart feeders. The base $99 model doesn't come with a solar roof or extended perch, as seen in the photo above, but you will get a 2K HDR camera that can shoot vertically or horizontally (it pops in and out via a magnet), as well as the same sturdy, high-quality construction as Birdbuddy's pricier Home model. The seed capacity isn't the greatest at 0.9 liters, but the app is easy to use and can even identify birds nearby that don't land on the feeder, so long as its excellent onboard microphone hears their sounds.

Birdbuddy's Achilles’ heel has always been its sensor, which is slow to wake up and regularly misses bird visits. The new Birdbuddy feeder supposedly has a faster wake-up time than previous models, and though it still lagged behind Birdfy's competing Rookie feeder in capturing all visits, the Nook's rate was substantially better than the Home's. It also has more mounting options, allowing for hanging in addition to wall and pole mounts (though the latter is a loose fit), and allows for no-cost manual AI ID of all visitors.

Camojojo's original Hibird feeder has long been a reliable model in my testing stable, one of the first to run on both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi bands, and last year saw the debut of an upgraded model, the Hibird Pro. The update has built-in solar panels, an option for pole-mounting, and supposedly improved AI identification, though it still frequently misidentifies even common birds in my West Coast backyard as East Coast species. The app is not as streamlined or user-friendly as Birdfy's or Birdbuddy's, but it's still easy enough to navigate, with options for changing video length (default is 10 seconds) or viewing in slo-mo. The default media type it saves is video, though this is 4K Ultra HD, and the images are—as expected—extremely sharp. Without a subscription, you can't search past videos by bird, and cloud storage is capped at 5 GB over 60 days; however, the feeder does come with a 128-GB SD card. You'll also get “smarter” chats with the app's AI Q&A function, “Dr. Bird,” and the ability to share across two devices with a subscription ($45 per year or $4 per month).

I appreciate the generous 1.5-liter seed hopper, although this, combined with the solar panel and battery, makes it extremely heavy. When filled, it tips the scales at 5 pounds, meaning that if you do pole-mount it, you will need to use both included hose clamps and wrench them tightly. I also wouldn't attempt to mount it on anything unstable, like a wobbly fence. Other original Hibird features that made it to the Pro include the little handles on the assembly screws (so you won't need any assembly tools) and the chunky plastic body. The latter was subjected to a little bit of squirrel-chewing during my test, but it still held up well.

The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 is one of the most thoughtfully designed feeders on the market. You don't have to take down the whole feeder when refilling, as the 1.5-liter dual-hopper plastic seed reservoir is removable from the body. The 8-megapixel photos and 4K HD video have much better quality than you'll find from most competitors, and the components come apart for easy cleaning. I also tested the original version, which features a separate solar panel, and my only complaint was that the panel stopped charging the camera after about six weeks. This version features a built-in solar roof, which did an excellent job keeping the feeder charged during its six-week-long test, even on cloudy days. The plastic body is extremely thick and sturdy, and unlike lighter-weight feeders like Birdfy's, it's designed to hold up in more extreme weather.

The app is easy to navigate, and the whole setup is functional without a Kiwibit Plus subscription ($90/year, purchasable online or through the Kiwibit app) but you'll be losing out on a lot of features, including 60-day storage and the ability to record up to three minutes of video if a bird is doing something interesting—a unique feature among smart feeders, and one I discovered that I love. (There's nothing more frustrating than having a video cut off right as a bird is about to do something funny.) This smart feeder costs a bit much for what it is, but if you know you like having a smart feeder, I think it's worth the investment. Note, however, that it only works on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi, and the warranty is half the length you get from many competitors. I also tested Kiwibit's newer model, the Feeder 2 Pro, and while its camera does have an interesting auto-zoom lens, I didn't think it was worth the $120 premium over this model.

Birdbuddy is known for its user-friendliness and thoughtful app—its Pro Smart Hummingbird Feeder is no exception. The feeder is intuitive and easy to use, and you don't need a subscription to access fun features like AI identification, 5 MP photos, and 2K HD video with slo-mo. A subscription unlocks features like family sharing and a higher bit rate, but the feeder is perfectly functional without those. With the panel being built into the feeder's roof, there’s also no auxiliary solar panel to worry about. Pairing with your phone is a cinch, integrating it into the Birdbuddy app with other feeders is a snap, and even refilling it is no problem. Unlike other hummingbird feeders that have weirdly cavernous capacities and/or need to be filled upside down, the Birdbuddy’s bottom screws off and holds a reasonable 1.75 cups of liquid. This detail is important; as the Cornell Lab of Ornithology points out, the easier it is to clean a hummingbird feeder, the more likely you are to do it often and well.

This feeder also comes with extra plastic flowers and a little brush for scrubbing them, and the app sends reminders when it's time to clean. You'll find fun, seasonal touches in the app, like the ability to send digital bird holiday cards with the photos your feeder captures, and a tool that superimposes hats, clothes, and various accessories on the birds, which is actually funnier than it sounds. However, as with the Birdbuddy seed feeders, the big downside is that the feeder's sensor doesn’t always pick up every bird that visits. This can definitely be a bummer, particularly when you see something interesting out the window but it doesn’t show up in the app.

After experiencing connection issues with the Birdfy Polygon, I swapped it out for the newer Birdfy Nest Duo and have had no issues. The sleek, contemporary Duo is a fir box fitted with two cameras—one facing the hole and one tucked discreetly inside the feeder. That gives you a full-spectrum view of what's going on. Both cameras have night vision (the internal one is infrared). Like the Polygon, the Duo sports a remote for rebooting and recharging the camera (though the separate solar panel, which can be pole-mounted, has kept the cameras reliably charged), as well as different-size holes for different species, each with its own chew-proof predator guard.

There's a metal grate with drainage holes that you can slot into grooves in the lower third of the Nest to make the cavity larger or smaller. The interested birds of my yard seemed very put off by the grate, so I covered it with a layer of craft mat moss, which was a success—a chickadee promptly moved in and laid seven eggs, all of which hatched. (I detail the experience in a separate review). For the first time, I was able to use the Birdfy app's ability to collect images from its nest boxes and string them together in a “story” that's shareable online. But I didn't find it especially useful or accurate. No matter, though, because the video captures have been a truly fascinating and educational experience, and I wish I could afford to buy the Duo for everyone I know.

So far, the Duo has been rained on a bunch and survived a couple of heat waves, but the wood finish and black paint are peeling and will need refinishing before I put them up for next season. (The feeder comes equipped with a thermometer and hygrometer to keep an eye on conditions. I recently had to zip-tie an umbrella to mine during a heat wave, which likely saved some fledglings' lives, though the lightweight construction and black-painted side and top probably contributed to the box overheating.)

I rarely expect (or get) compliments on my backyard smart feeders, but I have gotten many on this one, which has a distinctively modern look with natural wood (bamboo that's FSC-certified to be responsibly sourced) and a black-painted side and roof. It blends right into the landscape as opposed to providing a visual pop of plastic. (The pole and baffle shown in the photo above are not included.)

Birdfy's user-friendly app presents 2K HD images and video with free lifetime AI ID, and it's easy to share photos and videos with others. There's a solar panel you can mount separately, but I didn't do this and was impressed that the camera ran for nearly two months on an indoor USB-C charge.

Wood obviously comes with a higher risk of chewing by squirrels and other rodents, but there are metal guards available (both Birdfy-brand and aftermarket) that fit over the seed. I followed the 5-7-9 rule for pole-mounting to avoid this problem, but I was totally shocked at how weathered my feeder got after two months. And this was in a Pacific Northwest dry summer—about as mild as it gets. The finish was completely peeling off, so I recommend adding an extra layer of urethane (this is what I use) before putting it out for the first time, especially now, heading into winter.

Kiwibit’s new update to its original Feeder 2 is an interesting one; it’s the first bird feeder camera to feature autofocus in 4K HDR. The quality was exceptional, though, during my testing, some birds were alarmed by the camera movement. The biggest downside, though, is that most of this feeder’s features—including AI bird identification, expanded gallery views, and 60-day cloud storage—are now locked behind a $90-a-year paywall. It's not enough of an upgrade to justify paying the extra cash over the base-model Bird Feeder 2.

A lower-maintenance way to enjoy birds in your yard, this recycled-plastic birdbath comes outfitted with a dual-lens camera sending 1080p photos and 2K video via the Birdfy app and using the app’s AI capability for (free) bird identification. With the IP66-rated birdbath’s sturdy metal base (you can buy it for less without) and solar-powered battery and fountain pump, all you have to do is make sure the 3.5-liter, 1.65-inch reservoir is topped off with water. I've been using the Bath Pro for two seasons now, and while early connection issues have been resolved, the plastic has weathered, and the pump only works intermittently. I also find myself increasingly irritated with how long footage takes to load and how often the shallow plastic basin needs refilling and cleaning—every two or three days in dry weather. Still, if you're willing to put up with some quirks, the Bath Pro has been an entertaining and welcome addition to my bird-feeding setup.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? In my yard

Birdfy's unique flagship upgrade for 2025 won a CES Innovation Award and an American Good Design Gold Award. It features one dual-lens front-facing camera (2-MP/1080p wide-angle and 3-MP/2K portrait) and one 2-MP/1080p side camera. Both capture sharp, highly detailed video with high-quality sound. The front-facing camera even pans and crops to ensure the lens is focused on a bird. (Note that there's also a cheaper, single-camera version of the Feeder 2 that we haven't tested.) The feeder's IP66-rated plastic body, which has held up very well in Pacific Northwest winter weather, is wall-, pole-, or tree-mountable. An auxiliary solar panel and lifetime AI bird identification are both included. The reservoir holds slightly less seed than the original plastic Birdfy, at 42 ounces versus Birdfy 1’s 50 ounces. Overall, I was impressed with both the image quality and the Birdfy app's updated AI identification. That said, both cameras repeatedly dropped connections during my two-month testing period, even though I was using the required 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi network (only the Birdfy Metal 2 can run on 5 GHz). The solar panel, which requires separate mounting, also failed to keep the cameras consistently charged in cloudy weather.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? Office storage

This Kiwibit is thoughtfully designed, with a plastic seed reservoir that's removable from the body for refilling, so you don't have to take down the whole thing. Plus, the 3-watt solar panel can mount onto the back for pole installation, and the 8-MP photos and 4K HD video are much higher quality than what you'll find from many competitors. The whole setup is fully functional without a subscription, though opting in is necessary to access some features. The only downside of this version (without an integrated solar panel) is that the auxiliary solar panel stopped working after about six weeks. However, it's still a good deal if you don't mind having to bring it inside every few weeks to charge.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? Office storage

This feeder's VicoHome app leaves much to be desired, but its camera does get major points for staying fully charged for two months with its 3-watt built-in roof solar panel, despite getting very little sun in my Pacific Northwest backyard over the winter. Like many inexpensive feeder cameras, most of the Harymor's advertised features—such as AI identification and the ability to take 2K video—are hidden behind a subscription paywall. However, even upon activating the subscription, the AI was wrong more often than it was right.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? With fellow WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe

Birdbuddy's upgraded Home model comes with multiple design upgrades, including a little half-sphere–shaped camera that pops in and out with a magnet and an improved seed-filling hatch. You also have the ability to rotate the camera for a horizontal or vertical view, a feature borrowed from the CoolFly Aura. As with the Aura, I did not find this feature to be especially necessary or useful, but I did love how easy it was to install the camera. I was also impressed by how well it stayed charged via the solar roof. (Although in order to function properly, it did need a firmware update the first week I tried it.) However, my main problem with Birdbuddy has always been—and remains—the fact that the camera only captures a fraction of bird visits. In fact, while testing the Birdbuddy Home, I had it set up on a pole next to another brand's feeder. I saw out the window that birds often visited one feeder and then the other, but on a particularly active day I noted that the other feeder had 127 image captures, while the Birdbuddy Home had only one.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company

This feeder's got a generously sized dual-feed bay (4.2 cups on each side, for a total capacity of 8.4 cups); a built-in solar panel; an expandable perch; and a pretty solid 4-MP photo resolution, the clarity and quality of which were on par with more expensive cameras. There’s an option to view video in 0.5-speed slo-mo. As with most of the cheaper cameras, however, many of the features (like AI identification and video) are hidden behind a subscription. I didn’t find the ornithologist-trained AI identification to be super accurate, and the app was overall cumbersome to use, taking a while to load and then requiring multiple steps to engage the AI feature. I also didn't like that users must make an account that requires an address and phone number just to use the feeder, even if they’re not buying a premium plan. And if they are buying a premium plan, they can’t do it through the app store. They have to go through FeatherSnap’s website, which requires entering raw credit card info—no alternative payment options like PayPal or Apple Pay—and their address once again. It automatically charged my credit card at the end of the month-long subscription trial without warning, which was frustrating. There was no option to stop the recurring charge other than deleting my account.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? Office storage

I had high hopes for this feeder, my previous pick for Best Upgrade. Birdfy clearly had taken all the winning elements of other smart bird feeders—from its own line and from competitor products—and combined them into one tidy package. Tool-free assembly, 4K ultrahigh-definition video, the ability to run on 2.4-GHz or 5-GHz Wi-Fi, a chew-proof metal body, and enhanced AI ID that is more accurate than the standard version and can even identify different sexes: The Metal 2 had it all. It even looks great, with tasteful green tones and a natural wood perch. However, I have now been through two test units, and both have repeatedly disconnected from Wi-Fi, despite being next to the wall closest to my router. (And I will note the feeders were located in the same spot where I test all the smart feeders; this issue is rare, but similar to my eventual experience with Birdfy's Polygon nest box and Duo feeder.)

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? Office storage

Birdfy’s Hum Feeder Duo is the hummingbird-feeder version of the Duo seed feeder. Both editions of the Hum consist of a clear, BPA-free, anti-mold bottle that screws into a red base with a trio of plastic flowers. The duo has two 3-MP 2K cameras—one front-facing and one side-facing. The cameras charge together and provide a side-by-side view in the app. I had zero problems with setup. After an overnight charge, the feeder was up and running in about 10 minutes. One charge lasted a little over a week in Pacific Northwest November temperatures, though for $20 more, you can spring for the solar panel add-on with a patented ant moat (I have not yet tried this). I appreciate that the app shows battery life alongside temperature and humidity, which is helpful for gauging when to replace the liquid, although a more explicit notification like Birdbuddy's would be helpful. Like the seed feeder, however, my testing period was not without issue. In fact, I only had the Hum up for a couple of weeks before the sensor appeared to have failed, occasionally capturing wind-driven motion but failing to register any birds.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? Office storage

If you or a giftee is intimidated by the thought of a smart bird feeder, you may want to consider the Rookie. No complicated assembly, no solar panels, no tools—just snap three plastic pieces together, charge the camera, and you're ready to go. The whole setup reminds me of a gravity pet feeder. You'll have the same 1080p resolution as all other basic Birdfy cameras, but here the camera is mounted from the side. Half of the time, you'll only see a bird's back or butt. There's also no roof, meaning seeds will get wet in the rain (during my testing period, the lid even blew off with a gust of wind). You'll find some birds standing in the seed due to the lack of perch, which isn't great for disease spread. Battery life also wasn't stellar, down to 39 percent after only a week.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? Office storage

I love the style of this feeder, which looks like a contemporary condo and sports the same side-camera angle as the Rookie (left). Also like the Rookie, it's pretty simple—a 1080p camera and 1.3L seed hopper—and the camera angle ends up capturing a lot of bird butts. My main problem during the testing period, however, was durability. Birdfy doesn't specify the type of wood used in its construction, but it's very lightweight, almost like balsa wood. Even though I had it pole-mounted, it was knocked down and broken apart by squirrels within a week.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? Broken, but in office storage

Just when I thought I'd seen it all in the smart bird feeder world, CoolFly debuted a feeder with a modular camera system at CES 2026. Place the camera on either side of the broad perch: upright for a landscape view or on its side for closer-up portrait images. When I tested it, I really liked the easy-fill seed hopper and tool-free assembly, paired with quality 4-MP photos and 2.5K Ultra HD video. I did not, however, love the incessant marketing push notifications in the CoolFly app. The Aura also sports AI ID without a subscription, but this feature only works in one of the two camera modes, neither of which was different enough from the other to justify the hassle of switching between them. I also had to remove the metal seed grate that sits on top, as smaller birds were struggling to access the seed. That said, it's a perfectly fine feeder and was reliable in my tests, if you like the look.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? Office storage

Birdfy’s Polygon Smart Birdhouse is certainly unique-looking—the parallelogram-esque, turquoise-paneled shape won a Gold award at 2024’s French Design Awards—and it’s easy enough to mount on a pole, fence, or tree. All the camera equipment is located in an easy-to-open rear hatch, and there’s even a remote control at the end of a 10-foot cord to be able to charge or reset the 1080p camera (though it has a built-in solar panel, so I've never needed to do this). It's simple to integrate with the easy-to-use Birdfy app, which is ready and waiting to assemble a bird's shareable “story,” from building the nest to hatching to fledgling, and finally “the end,” when the nest is abandoned for the season. Note that the camera does emit an audible click whenever movement or the app triggers it, and when I had a chickadee interested in the nest, the bird clearly heard this and found it alarming. I have had consistent connectivity issues over the two seasons I've used the Polygon, so if you're in the market for a smart nesting box, I recommend the Birdfy's Nest Duo instead, which is both more fun and more reliable for around $50 extra.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? Office storage

If you have a non-smart bird feeder you already like, or are interested in building your own and are just looking for a camera, Hibird's stand-alone DIY feeder camera is what you want. It's compatible with both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi bands and has better-than-average-quality 4K HD video and 32 MP photos. There is a subscription tier with features like increased storage and the ability to share livestreams, but the camera is still usable without it. There's an auxiliary solar panel included for charging, and you can mount it via its quarter-inch nut on the included bendable arm and bracket, or jury-rig a custom solution.

How was test unit obtained? Press sample from company Where is it now? Office storage

Assembly of this birdbath is easy and intuitive, and it’s lightweight and small enough that you can put it on a taller pole to avoid leaves and debris, as I did. The fountain is quite vigorous, and the solar panel works well to keep the 2K camera charged. However, the build quality is notably inferior to Birdfy’s similarly priced entry, and you only get stills unless you lock yourself into a subscription with VicoHome.

What to Look for When Buying a Smart Bird Feeder

The world of smart bird feeders is vast and can seem overwhelming, but there are some key features that will really make a difference in your user experience. I've tested dozens of feeders for years from many different brands, and this is what I think you should pay attention to when comparing models.

Subscription: Most, if not all, smart bird feeders require a subscription to access all features. That's in order to support the company's continued investment in user experience. There are few things more disappointing than giving or receiving a smart bird feeder as a gift, only to find out it's not actually usable without shelling out an additional $70 a year. Reputable companies will note subscription requirements up front, and some even offer models that have a lifetime subscription built in. Note that if a feeder costs less than a hundred bucks, odds are it will require a subscription to capture photos, whether it says so in the marketing materials or not. You will need to do your due diligence before buying.

Mounting options: If you live in an area with squirrels, your best bet is to pole-mount your bird feeder—especially a more expensive smart feeder, which often has cords that squirrels and other rodents like to chew. Not all feeders offer a pole-mounting option, though, which is another important detail to confirm before buying.

Wi-Fi network: The vast majority of smart feeders only work on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi frequencies. If you only use 5 GHz, you will need to look for a feeder that specifically works with a shorter transmission range or has dual range, such as the Camojojo Hibird, above.

App: An app can make or break your smart bird feeder experience since it's where all of your bird viewing, sorting, and saving will take place. Apps with added features like useful facts, the capacity to share feeds with others, quality AI identification, and the ability to sort by bird are sometimes worth the added cost over a less-expensive feeder. Many companies use security cameras in their bird feeders that don't have a separate app—this means you'll just get a utilitarian list of image captures with no detail or context. To help buyers with their decision-making, I am currently building a rubric to grade and rank smart bird feeder apps, which I hope to add to this guide within the next couple of months.

I test all feeders in my rural-suburban backyard in the Pacific Northwest. I mount seed feeders on a 1-inch pole with a baffle, using the provided mounting hardware and hose clamps. If pole-mounting isn't feasible, I mount on a fence or a shepherd's hook. I hang hummingbird feeders from a shepherd's hook mounted on the side of my house. I fill the seed feeders with Audubon Wild Park bird seed and the hummingbird feeders with a nectar mixture of 4-to-1 granulated sugar and water. I keep each feeder up for a minimum of four weeks, with all app notifications enabled.

I look at all app features available both with a subscription and without, seeing how often I get notifications and noting whether they are accurately picking up just birds or any type of outdoor movement, and how well the AI feature is able to distinguish bird species. I also look at connectivity, seed capacity, video quality, and how well the feeder bodies hold up to squirrels and inclement weather.

The majority of feeders I tested were provided as press samples by the company. I keep some for longer-term testing, put others in storage for future testing or comparison purposes, and donate others locally via the Buy Nothing Project.

What Do I Need to Know Before Setting Up a Smart Feeder?

Why Do Most Smart Feeders Only Run on 2.4 GHz?

This section was inspired by an email from a reader who installs home Wi-Fi systems and did not appreciate my recommending a feeder that has the option to run on 5 GHz. He's not wrong that this isn't the preferred band for a smart bird feeder, but I'll explain why someone might want 5 GHz below.

First off, what is 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz? In simplest terms, these are the main radio frequency bands Wi-Fi uses to send data wirelessly between your smart bird feeder and your router. One gigahertz (GHz) is 1 billion hertz, the unit of measurement for how fast radio waves oscillate. Both bands are the accepted standards for Wi-Fi, which yes, is a name brand.

It follows, then, that 2.4-GHz waves oscillate more slowly than 5-GHz waves. This also means the slower waves can travel farther and pass through walls and other obstacles more effectively. With Wi-Fi-enabled products placed outside the home, the ability to penetrate walls, trees, and other potential barriers is more important than speed. These slower waves also result in less power consumption by devices. It makes sense that 2.4 GHz would be a preferable band for a smart bird feeder, which likely would be in or near a tree-filled area.

However, 2.4 GHz is a more crowded band and thus prone to interference from other Wi-Fi networks and devices, so it can be less stable. It also results in slower overall performance, leading to sluggish downloads and lag during streaming and video calls. Most modern routers offer both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands, but some may be configured (for whatever reason) to broadcast only 5 GHz. Other routers feature something called band steering, which automatically diverts devices to the less-crowded 5 GHz. A smart bird feeder that offers dual connectivity simply provides more options. If the bird feeder is right outside your window where the router is located, you may want the faster speed. Or maybe you just don't want to try to figure out how to turn off band steering. If you're not dialed in to your router, no pun intended, it may make sense for you to consider a bird feeder with dual-band connectivity.

As is the case with any bird feeder, squirrels love to eat at smart bird feeders, most of which are not squirrel-proof, regardless of marketing claims. However, most of the smart feeders we’ve tested are just as sturdy, if not in some cases sturdier, than analog bird feeders. The worst-case scenario is likely the squirrel eating all the seed, chewing the edges, and covering up the camera with its fuzzy butt.

The yard where I test smart feeders year-round is lousy with the large and persistent rodents, and the squirrel damage I’ve sustained on test feeders has been minor. With the Birdfy Pro Duo, above, the animals chewed off the edges to better get at the seed supply when it was low, and the FeatherSnap Scout had its mounting bent. Top of mind is the 5-7-9 method of siting a bird feeder—at least 5 feet off the ground, at least 7 feet away from any structures, and at least 9 feet away from anything a squirrel could jump from (branches, fences, roofs). I explain this in more detail in my guide to keeping squirrels away from your bird feeder.

Another option is an aftermarket baffle added to feeders hanging on shepherd’s hooks, or a pole with a built-in baffle, like this one from Birdfy. Or you could use seed treated with capsaicin, or hot pepper. The taste doesn't affect birds, since they don’t have capsaicin receptors like mammals do. That said, I’ve found capsaicin only keeps squirrels away for a couple of days, whether because they’ve gotten used to it or the pepper loses its potency when exposed to the elements. As a last resort, you could always just learn to live with the squirrels and dedicate a feeder to them, although my neighbor does this, and I'm of the mind that doing so brings even more squirrels to the area.

#395. What to know about this year’s UN climate talks

Climate finance and fossil fuels top the formal agenda at COP31.

It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.

One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.

The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.

With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.
