#373. Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?

I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind.

These thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the company is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy.

WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: Lauren, first of all, thank you for your tirelessness these past few days. The last time I saw you, we were both in Miami for WIRED’s big event, and you were getting on a red-eye that night to go to Europe for vacation, which didn’t exactly go as planned. When you saw that first story about Jensen’s affair on Sunday, what did you think? What went through your mind?

LAUREN GOODE: Oof. The story first started bubbling up a while ago because The New York Times, and a lot of credit is due to The New York Times here, first reported on Nvidia’s relationship, if you want to call it that, with this company Megaspeed, back in the fall of 2025.

It was a very unusual story. And for some reason it just didn’t capture the attention of people the way that more recent reporting that we and others have been doing has.

Anyone who’s sort of been paying attention to that story, or had some sources in the industry, were starting to hear things. But the fact that the affair with this person, who goes by Alice Huang, was confirmed, that’s the kind of story that always captures people’s attention in a different way.

There are few things people love to read about more than extramarital affairs, especially when they involve powerful people. The reason it wasn’t surprising to you, was it because of that previous reporting and what you had been hearing here and there? Or was there another reason that you saw that story and thought, “OK, actually some of this is not shocking to me”?

It was both. I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but in the fall of 2024 we were doing a WIRED outing, a few of us hanging out, and we started chatting about whether or not we thought a lot of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley had girlfriends or extramarital affairs or situations. Because there are some people in Silicon Valley who are actually quite open about that. I remember us talking about it at the time, and there’s part of me that always kind of assumes that there are elements of their personal lives that we’re never going to have a full window into.

Not that we were talking about Jensen that evening, but it’s always been in my mind. Then, yes, I think being on the ground in Silicon Valley, you often hear things. But a lot of times there’s a certain threshold that things have to cross in order for us as journalists to consider something reportable or something worth chasing down as reportable.

I think an important distinction is that people cheat, people have affairs all the time, Silicon Valley or otherwise.

What tips this over into newsworthiness is, A) the Chinese espionage of it all, and B) the affair with a subordinate.

You reported that Jensen’s resignation—which really, to be clear, is the board of Nvidia ousting him—probably had more to do with the alleged affair with a subordinate than this other extramarital relationship, which is tied up in espionage allegations. A source told you this. Can you explain why that affair would tip the balance for the board?

I just think it’s important to note that this doesn’t seem like it was simply a moral decision. Someone had posted on X that “I can't believe the board caved to moral pressure.” To me, this doesn’t seem like it’s a moral issue.

I think if you’re looking at the three things that could have led to serious scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s behavior, there’s: One, extramarital affairs. Two, alleged extramarital affairs with subordinates within his own company. And three, an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese operative, which puts Jensen Huang in this position where the board and the investigators who are looking into this are trying to determine what he knew and when he knew it, and basically whether he was aware of the fact that chips were making their way into China.

This isn’t just about the fact that someone had a girlfriend outside of their marriage. I think what is still to be revealed here could in fact be very, very serious in nature.

Now, you also reported on Monday, in a fantastic scoop for WIRED, that Jensen hired a crisis comms firm a year ago. In October 2025 he hired a fixer, Risa Heller, who is very well known for working with high-profile men who are facing allegations of sexual misconduct, among other things. I’m talking about Anthony Weiner, Mario Batali, writer Jeffrey Toobin. Tell us a little bit about that story and what you found out.

I really feel like with everything else going on this week, I could have gone without ever hearing about all of those stories again.

Oh, you don’t want to hear about Anthony Weiner all the time?

No, it turns out. I had kind of forgotten that. I was like, “I think I blocked that from my memory.” And Jeff Toobin—what a throwback.

But this firm, it’s a really interesting firm run by this woman named Risa Heller. They have offices in New York and LA, and yes, they have this reputation for dealing with a lot of sexual misconduct cases, as well as other types of corporate and personal PR needs for high-profile people.

A source had told me a while ago, and I’m not gonna timestamp it, but a while ago that it had been rumored that Jensen Huang had hired this firm. So immediately my antenna went up, and I was like, “Wait, what?”

I thought it was curious, but I didn’t know exactly what the nature of the contract was or when they had been hired, and then eventually through more reporting, I was able to get confirmation of some of the details.

What we know is that this firm, Heller, started working with Jensen Huang sometime in 2025, and ostensibly, Huang and his family had hired Heller for their own personal PR outside of Nvidia’s walls. This is because when you’re someone like Jensen Huang, you have a lot going on. You have a family office. You do a lot of work with philanthropy. You’re hosting personal events. He’s also been grooming his adult children to take over these higher profile roles within Nvidia, so some of the PR might have ostensibly been to work on creating more of a public-facing image for his kids.

We do know, though, based on more reporting, that as of October 2025, and then closer to the end of the year, Nvidia’s internal teams had been instructed to start looping this outside crisis firm, Heller, into all press inquiries, all communications related to Jensen.

That was definitely a change from the prior terms of his working relationship with Heller, and also timing-wise coincided with that first New York Times story I mentioned. I think that it was published on October 9th, 2025, and first highlighted Megaspeed and what appeared to be a very close relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang.

I can’t decide if he should get his money back for hiring this crisis comms firm, because this crisis has certainly not been contained, or if the fact that this is now coming up a year later suggests that maybe they did their job quite well for a while.

Well, first of all, I don’t think he needs the money back.

… on how his assets get divided, yes. Or if maybe they won’t divorce. You know, it’s also a very Silicon Valley thing not to necessarily do that.

I also think it’s possible that Jensen himself was not totally upfront with this firm when he hired them. Or, if they knew something was up, they may not have known all of the details. So if that is the case, hypothetically, then you can’t necessarily do everything you would typically do in terms of reputation management. TL;DR, it didn’t work out so well for him in the end.

No, things are not going well for Jensen. Now, Nvidia has named an interim CEO to replace him. Surprise, surprise, to both of us and women everywhere, she’s a woman.

What do we know about Colette Kress, who is the interim CEO of Nvidia?

Well, we know that when we emailed Jensen this summer to say, “Hey, Jensen, who do you think the most powerful women in Silicon Valley are?” He didn't mention Colette. Jensen mentioned Dina Powell from Meta and Ruth Porat from Google, both really high-ranking women, presidents of those companies.

And then [SpaceX president and COO] Gwynne Shotwell, because I prompted him. But no Colette, and that struck me as interesting at the time, too, though I didn’t press him on that. And then we did end up giving Colette a nod in our big feature that we did about high-ranking women in Silicon Valley.

Colette has been with Nvidia since 2013. Prior to that, she worked at Cisco, Microsoft. She’s CFO. She’s a financial whiz. She’s the person who appears on earnings calls with him every quarter.

She actually does a lot of the speaking, because she’s a person who has really, really deep knowledge of Nvidia’s complex financials. She’s the person who gives guidance for the next quarter. She’s CFO of arguably the world’s most important company. I think it makes sense that she would be slotted into this role.

Nvidia doesn’t really have a traditional hierarchy. They don’t have a traditional chief operating officer, for example. You know, when Steve Jobs was at the end of his tenure and he was very sick, Tim Cook, who was the operations whiz at Apple for many years prior, was basically groomed to be the CEO.

Nvidia doesn’t have someone like that. So it makes sense for now that Colette is the person who would slot in, because part of Nvidia’s goal has to be, at this point, easing the stock market. I don’t know if you’ve been following, but, I mean, it’s pretty bad out there.

I would say that, against my will, I am seeing a lot about Nvidia stock not doing well. I have not looked at my 401(k). I try really hard not to because I’m a control freak, and I simply cannot control how many affairs this man is having and what impact that has on my finances.

These things, though, help paint a picture of Jensen’s character and the way he ran the company. The fact that Nvidia did not do succession planning. There was no hierarchy; he had dozens of direct reports. There was no successor waiting in the wings. What do those things combined tell us about Jensen and Nvidia?

As I understand it, Katie, even you have had to do a succession plan, right?

Yes, without revealing too many details, Condé Nast, like most normal companies, has people in senior leadership roles do succession planning. They take it really seriously. It’s an annual exercise that we do, and my understanding is that that is very par for the course at most companies, at any company, and particularly a company of Nvidia’s stature and importance on a global scale. The idea that there would not be a formal succession plan is shocking to me.

It is shocking, and it’s shocking not just from the perspective that Jensen perhaps didn’t do that or didn’t have a super well-formulated one, but that the board wouldn’t demand that. I’ve heard a few different theories floated as to why this is. One theory is that Jensen may have had a lot of the insecurities that come with being a cofounder, CEO, someone who’s been living and breathing this company, his baby, since 1993, and not necessarily wanting to stuff the ranks with people who are just as capable, if not more capable in some measures, than himself, right?

Like you don’t create an environment in which someone could theoretically replace you that easily. So that’s one theory. The other theory is that—and Jensen himself has said this, both to me and other people in interviews too—he truly believed that keeping a flat org was better for the flow of information, that once you start to create a structure that’s too hierarchical, then any kind of changes that happen in the company, any kind of new information that comes out, even in some kind of white paper, fundamentally changes the direction of the way the industry is going.

I mean, think about the way people inside the AI industry probably reacted when they first saw the famous Transformer paper in 2017 and said, “Oh my gosh, this is going to change everything.” If you’re a big, fat, bloated, slow organization, you’re probably five years behind on your AI strategy. If you’re lean at the top, you can basically say, “Let’s go. We’re going in this direction now,” and you won’t encounter a lot of barriers to doing that. So that helps explain the flat org. It doesn’t necessarily explain the lack of a succession plan.

The third theory that’s been floated to me is that maybe in some, I don’t know, alternate universe, he really did think that his children, one of his two children, who are both working within Nvidia, would one day be the inevitable successors.

You have met Jensen several times. You’ve corresponded with him, you’ve interviewed him, you published a cover story for WIRED that featured an excellent interview with him. You published an edition of our newsletter, Backchannel, at the end of last week with a little bit about this. In it you talk about one experience you had interviewing Jensen at a conference. You wrote, “Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me.” You describe him as obsessed with controlling the narrative.

Again, we’re coming back to this theme of control. I’m curious to hear a little bit more about that observation, this idea of Jensen as fixated on storytelling and the stories that were told about Nvidia and about AI.

That particular interview was July of 2024, and Nvidia had invited me to interview Jensen again at the SIGGRAPH Conference in Denver, which is this whole confab of computer graphics nerds. It’s a really fun conference.

During the preparation for it, when I got on the call with some Nvidia comms executives, Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter, appeared on the call and she basically took the lead and said, “Here’s this cluster of slides that when you’re on stage, Jensen’s going to be referencing, and he’s gonna have a lot to say about each slide, and it would be great if you could tee him up at this point.”

And I said, “Well, wait a second. This is not a standard journalistic interview. Like, what’s going on here?” The whole thing felt very strange, but I made it clear I planned to ask him the questions I really felt I needed to ask him as a journalist. It was just very clear he did not want to answer a lot of my questions, and that he was going to just own the stage and reference his slides. I remember that he talked about how he made a little Jensen AI of himself, and the crowd was all, “Ha! Jensen AI,” and I was like, “What is happening?”

It was so strange. Afterwards, he did this impromptu Q&A with the crowd. A bunch of people rushed the stage. I could see someone from his PR team being like, “What just happened? What is he doing?” Not standard operating procedure. I thought, wow. It felt to me like Jensen Huang was just riding high on this wave, this AI wave and this incredible success that Nvidia was experiencing and the way the AI industry was growing.

But it occurred to me that he was really, really obsessive with controlling the narrative, and it reminded me of something that he’d said the first time we’d ever spoken, which was that he really admired the CEO of Adobe because he felt that the CEO of Adobe was a very good storyteller, and that he never had a pitch deck when he first pitched Nvidia as a company because he just thought it was better to tell a story.

Storytelling is so important in terms of establishing the culture of a company. He was very good at creating his own story, his own image of himself as this founder CEO who was utterly obsessed with his own company and really passionate about everything.

I guess we know where some of that passion led him.

We do indeed. It’s interesting that you talk about Jensen as a crowd favorite, because he did very much become that. He’s incredibly charismatic. He’s a great public speaker. He can really own a room. He can spin a great yarn. You describe in the cover story about Jensen, that you were “Jensen-pilled” after spending time with him, because he is so compelling.

That was interesting to me this week, in seeing how many leaders in Silicon Valley came out in support of him, despite these very, very troubling allegations, which to be clear, again, go beyond having an affair. This is beyond moral decision-making. Regardless of that, everyone from Elon Musk to Jason Calacanis came out guns blazing for Jensen.

Do you think that speaks to how revered he is in the industry, or do you think that that speaks to the fact that he is mission-critical for the industry’s ongoing growth? Are these defenses of Jensen essentially self-interested on the part of industry leaders?

I don't think they’re all self-interested. There are at least three layers to this, and one is that there are executives and lower-level tech workers who have worked for Jensen directly, and who came away from the experience with not a great taste in their mouths. They left feeling uninspired, and they actually saw a more egotistical side of him that they didn’t like, an obsessive side. There have been stories reported by other outlets about how he has sometimes berated some of his top lieutenants in front of other people. There’s almost a Dr. Jensen and Mr. Huang narrative here. He’s got two sides to him. But he’s very smart and almost can come across as sort of mensch-y. I think people really admire him.

Then I think, yes, there are people who probably own Nvidia stock, they’re industry watchers, they’re tech enthusiasts, and they see him perhaps still as a kind of our generation’s rock star who also happens to be keeping the economy afloat with his company.

I will say WIRED had a great scoop last week, much credit to our amazing journalists, of Nvidia employees who would like to see Jensen back. There is a great deal of reverence for him, in a way that I have to admit gave me acute flashbacks to 2023, when Sam Altman was ousted at OpenAI. Very different circumstances, but yet again, a woman was installed to clean up that mess, and employees revolted and called for Sam to come back. I mean, these allegations are much more significant and serious and consequential. That said, the jury’s still out on whether Jensen makes a comeback in two weeks.

Wow. OK. I would be very surprised. We should make a bet.

Oh, Lauren. I was going to say dinner the next time I’m in San Francisco.

Dinner sounds good. Let’s do it. You know what? Whoever loses the bet has to buy dinner at Proposition Chicken, which according to, was it the Daily … ?

The Daily Mail reported that Proposition Chicken, which is a slightly elevated fast food chicken place in San Francisco, was being delivered to Jensen Huang’s house in Pacific Heights the other day.

OK. I’m in. Two weeks from today, we will see.

I want to ask you lastly about ripple effects. Nvidia has invested in or bought outright plenty of AI startups. It finances a lot of the build-out happening in this industry. I have been stomping around the New York office all week screaming things like, “The global economy, the global economy!” I mean, this is much bigger than just this company, right? So what are the industry effects that we should all be watching out for from here?

What I’ve heard so far from people is that in the short term—even though we’re seeing this dip right now—there’s still just such incredible demand for Nvidia chips, and they plan everything basically 18 to 24 months out in terms of producing those chips, that I don’t think we’ll see any really serious softness in Nvidia in the short term.

But I think that the long tail of Nvidia is going to be interesting, because another CEO could come in with a totally different approach to how Nvidia spends its capital and how it also makes investments in outside companies.

Would a new CEO come in right now and make the kind of investment in CoreWeave or Perplexity, for example, that Jensen decided to? Quite possibly no. Would the new CEO come in and decide to spend so much on, let’s say, Nvidia’s healthcare division? We don’t really know. Would the new CEO come in and be as much of an open source booster as Jensen Huang had become? We don’t really know.

It’s just hard to say. The guys at Hugging Face are probably quite happy that they got in when they did.

Another thing that Jensen had set Nvidia on the path of in the past couple years was really investing in what they’re doing with CPUs as well as GPUs, which is an area that Intel and AMD are in, as well as Arm.

Was that the right path to set the company on, to over-index a little bit on CPUs for now because of the ways that the AI industry is shifting from training on high-powered GPUs to inference computing on slightly lower-powered CPUs? I think it was a smart move, but let’s see how that shakes out.

I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but back in 2008, shortly after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, a venture capitalist at Sequoia sent around a pitch deck to all of that firm’s portfolio companies that became very famous in the industry, and it’s called “RIP Good Times.”

In that pitch deck, this very prescient VC basically laid out all of the things that they wanted their portfolio companies to do, which meant saving a lot of cash. Like, this is a gird-your-loins moment. I think if we see something like that kind of mentality start to develop in Silicon Valley in the coming weeks and months, then I think that’s a very big indication that people are genuinely worried about what this Nvidia tumble means.

I am going to ask you to make one final prediction.

OK. I’m very bad at predictions, by the way, but please.

Two years ago, you said, “Huang is the man of the hour. The year. Maybe even the decade.” I would argue that that decade has been cut short, but I also think that someone like Jensen doesn’t just go quietly into the night. If he’s not reinstalled at Nvidia, and I’m wrong, and I’m buying your chicken in two weeks, where does someone like that go? Where do you expect we will see Jensen pop up in a year, in two years?

There’s a glib answer and it’s either Jensen goes to jail, or Jensen starts a podcast. I’m sure he’s hoping right now it’s the podcast outcome.

Realistically, let’s say that he’s not implicated in the end result of any kind of federal investigation. And let’s say he’s not reinstated. In either case, I don’t think this is the last we’re going to hear from Jensen Huang.

#372. Building AI that can work across the enterprise

Moving AI beyond isolated pilots requires a strong data foundation, clear business outcomes, and governance built for enterprise scale.

For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model.

For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.”

That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can't scale is just an experiment,” he says.

Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn't speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit.

Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.

This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys.

Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I'm Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.

This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys.Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we're still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI's value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It's becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can't simply be added into an enterprise's existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what's inside and how it's used.

Two words for you: conscious configuration.My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy.Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder.

Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation.

We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation. Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example. When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack?

Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation.This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale. At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed. This is also shown in some studies. For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization.The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes.

Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we're seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What's the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well?

Satinder: Absolutely, Megan. And, if anything, the picture sharpens when you look at, specifically, at agentic AI. Infosys and HFS research surveyed over 500 global 2,000 enterprises and found only 14% have successfully scaled AI. Eighty-six percent remain in early exploration, proof of concept, or fragmented pilot phases. For a technology at the top of every boardroom agenda for two years, that's a striking failure rate. And at the core of that 86% is what I would describe as AI as a department trap.

What happens is that an organization creates an AI team or a center of excellence and walls it off from business. That team builds technically excellent pilots the business doesn't recognize itself in, and you end up with AI solutions searching for problems, rather than the other way around. Mindset shift is clear. Move from treating AI as a technology initiative to treating it as an operating model transformation. AI stops being something IT does for business and starts being something the whole organization does together. Every function, every workflow, embedded from the start.

And what makes this a now problem? Early movers are building an advantage. You cannot close by buying the same platform later. Eighteen months of agent behavior data, calibrated knowledge graph, workforce that has genuinely internalized AI, that is a structural advantage that compounds. Infosys Knowledge Institute AI Maturity Index shows that only 8% of the companies qualify as AI native today, yet they achieve four times the revenue contribution from the AI versus laggards. If you're not building AI today, you're not standing still, you're falling behind at an accelerating rate.

Megan: Right. There's a real polarization there, isn't there, between the front-runners and the laggards, as you say. As we shift from pilot to scaled-up applications, perhaps the first step is evaluating when AI is the right tool. AI has quickly become the default solution within many enterprises. Thorsten: Yeah, I think, Megan, what everybody needs to be aware is adopting and rolling out AI across an organization is as much a change management journey as it's a technology rollout.Now, when you have this in mind, it makes absolutely sense to put AI in front as many teams as possible, because you want to build formality, and spark ideas, and also people should see the benefit of AI in an organization. When you think about travel assistance, meeting summaries via Copilot, or AI-enabled workflows, increase the productivity, everybody feels this in their real job, in their real daily business. Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten's framing of AI agents as digital coworkers forces a precision that agentic AI strategy language often lacks. Thorsten: Yeah, Megan, I think the fundamental, which many organizations are overlooking, is data and the data is a foundation for AI. Megan: Which is so important, because when organizations are experimenting with, or scaling up multiple AI programs and tools, in some cases, it adds real complexity. Satinder: We, at Infosys, have our Infosys Knowledge Institute, they run this annual magazine generative AI radar, and it found that 48% of companies had deployed generative AI without a formal governance policy. Nearly half of the enterprises were running AI with no documented framework or oversight, accountability, or compliance. This needs legal, compliance, technology teams together with a board level sponsorship. Without that foundation, every deployment becomes an ad hoc governance debate. Second layer is platform. Thorsten: I think what we will see very soon, and we talked about this briefly, is that we are heading into a period of sustained, rapid AI adoption, where assistance and agents will operate as digital coworkers. They will be embedded in our organizations like employees today, and they will be embedded into processes as people perform tasks, as we speak.Now, as this happens, the Center of Gravity will shift more and more from a monolithic application layer to an agentic value layer that orchestrates work across systems and across different landscapes, which need to be orchestrated very well. I think what we also will see, and this will be likely, at least in terms of scale, I believe a game-changer, is that the delivery will become industrialized. When you think about agent factories and church services that really design, test, and govern agents at scale, or you can say agentic frameworks at scale, and I think we will see an evolution of commercial models, which are today more consumption-based towards really value and outcome-based agreements, which are then tied to clear business KPIs.On the technology front, I think there's still so much movement on the LLM landscape, new architectures, training methods. I think we'll bring down, significantly, the total cost of ownership, while also control and the viability will be improved. I think there's an awareness which the recent examples in the market show, and then I think the innovation will be playable.And I think the big question is, from that perspective, which role is China going to play in a global context, and also how those models are really embedded. Last but not least, most importantly, even I think ontology and customer-specific knowledge graphs will become first-class assets, and I think this will be the key differentiation in the future, because they will lead in code process, semantics, policies, what Satinder talked about, and data relationships. And they are the blueprint for secure high-performing enterprise agent architectures in the future.

For decades, enterprise systems have told us what happened. The next generation helps leader understand what is happening now, what will happen next, what actions to take.

The scenario I keep coming back to, a CFO starting a day with an agent that continuously analyzes signals across finance, supply chain, procurement, workforce data, proactively surfacing the three issues that are most likely to impact the quarter, with recommended actions, financial impact quantified. That's not a dashboard. That's a fundamentally different decision model. Through Infosys Topaz, we are helping clients move forward an AI-first enterprise, one that can sense, learn, decide, adapt continuously across the different domains.

What also excites me is the pace of AI evolution. In past technology waves, constraints were stable. You identify a limitation and architect around it for years. AI is different. Use cases that appear constrained at program start are often resolved before go live. SAP's prior model transformed structured data reasoning once a clear LLM gap. Decision intelligence is arriving faster than most organization are planning for.

The winning strategy is to design for where AI will be 18 months from now, flexible architecture, trusted data foundation, governance that absorbs innovation as it arrives. Organizations that do this compound value at each new generation of capabilities becomes available.

#371. Could Jensen Huang return to Nvidia? What Trump, Altman, the board are saying.

For 33 years, Nvidia had only one CEO. Now, just days after the chipmaker announced Jensen Huang's resignation, some of the country's biggest names are already want him back — from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to President Donald Trump.

The decision ultimately belongs to Nvidia's board, which has appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO.

The calls for a comeback follow a week of mounting scrutiny over Huang's intimate extracurriculars. On Nov. 8, Huang had told employees he’d been unfaithful to his wife after reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company that buys Nvidia chips. U.S. officials suspect she had ties to Chinese intelligence, an allegation Beijing has denied. The same day Huang emailed employees, Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Reuters also reported that Huang had relationships with two Nvidia employees, including one who reported directly to him. Inhales.

It's a lot. But that doesn't mean everyone thinks its enough to get rid of the co-founder permanently. On Nov. 15, Huang was already talking to people close to him about a possible return, according to the Financial Times. One ally told the paper they were getting tech executives together to lobby for his reinstatement and would seek support from the White House.

On Monday, Trump gave that effort some encouragement. "I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters before leaving Washington for the Philippines and China. He said he thought Huang had "learned a big lesson" and questioned whether Alice Huang had worked for Chinese intelligence.

A day earlier, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Larry Kudlow on Fox News that Nvidia should hire its next CEO from outside the company, saying it needed a "dramatic shake-up."

Huang's supporters are also making their case online. "Thirty-three years deserve an answer," reads the Stand With Jensen petition, which demands that Nvidia's board reinstate its co-founder while the independent investigation is underway. "We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process," it adds. If directors think Huang should stay out of the job, the letter asks them to explain what evidence led them to that decision and why it serves Nvidia's interests. It also calls on the board to disclose what the investigation will cover, when it expects to finish, and how Huang will get a chance to respond. By Monday afternoon, the campaign's website showed more than 185,000 signatures, including more than 9,300 from people who identified themselves as current Nvidia employees. The site also lists Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad among the signers.

The push to bring Huang back is familiar territory for OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. OpenAI's board fired him in Nov. 2023, and he returned days later after employees and investors rallied behind him. At Semafor's Silicon Valley & the World event on Monday, Altman said he sympathized with Huang and had long seen him as a hero. When asked whether Huang should get his job back, Altman said, "I don’t think I know enough to answer that question." He added: "it's hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen Huang."

Altman also sounded confident in Nvidia's ability to back the data centers that AI companies depend on. "Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company," he said. "I think people still trust their guarantees very much."

OpenAI has a stake in that confidence. At an Ohio data center campus where an OpenAI affiliate is leasing capacity, Nvidia has agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion in certain lease and power payments if the tenant defaults under conditions spelled out in the deal. The campus is set to run on Nvidia hardware, with limited exceptions.

For now, Kress is running Nvidia on an interim basis while keeping the CFO job she's held since 2013. The board, led by longtime director Harvey C. Jones, says it will consider internal and external candidates. It has already approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, the Financial Times reported.

The next chance to hear from Nvidia's new leadership comes Tuesday at 5 p.m. ET, when the company holds its first earnings call since Huang's departure.

#369. Nvidia Scandal Unleashes a Flood of AI-Generated Memes

The revelations surrounding Jensen Huang, who resigned from Nvidia over extramarital affairs, inspired social media posts using the very technology his company helped develop.

Jensen Huang and his leather-clad likeness had become synonymous with the technological giant he co-founded, Nvidia. They were so entwined that, this year, the company sold $178 sweaters with a pixel-art version of Mr. Huang on the front.

Now, in the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday after back-to-back cheating scandals, including an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy, the internet has taken ahold of his image to unleash a flood of memes.

In many cases, they are being made by A.I. enthusiasts who revered Mr. Huang.

Images of Mr. Huang have appeared in online parodies of music videos, Bollywood movies, American sitcoms and kiss-cams at Coldplay concerts — many generated using artificial intelligence, the technology that became widely available through the chips Nvidia produces.

The revelations about Mr. Huang, 63, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom, are part of a long list of infidelity scandals that became memes.

Last year, the married chief executive of a tech start-up was caught on a kiss-cam at a Coldplay concert embracing the married but separated head of his company’s human resources department.

Mr. Huang’s image was superimposed on that viral moment by Peter Dedene, a Belgian software engineer. He said in a phone interview on Thursday that he was up late this week on his phone, scrolling the headlines about Nvidia.

#368. AO3 Is Back. This Is Not a Drill

Dust off that Hitachi and put your Slack on “Do not disturb,” because AO3 is back online, baby.

After weeks off the internet due to an unspecified security incident, the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit that runs the hugely popular fan fiction forum, announced on November 15 that service had been restored.

“We understand that the wait and uncertainty surrounding AO3’s return have been difficult, and we apologize for the inconvenience,” the statement reads. “We greatly appreciate your support during the downtime, and continued patience as our volunteers work hard to return AO3 to its full functionality.”

The news came as a pleasant surprise to AO3’s devoted fans, as the website had announced in late October that restoring service could take between two to four weeks. To that end, the OTW statement says that some of the site’s features, such as user icons and external work importing, have been temporarily disabled in order to expedite the site’s return. It also warned that users “may experience a delay before AO3 loads,” due to “high traffic.”

Founded in 2007, AO3 is one of the most popular fan fiction forums on the internet, boasting more than 11 million users and over 18 million original works. Following its temporary shutdown, many devastated fans started sharing Google Docs of their favorite fanfics, sparking some concerns among authors worried about AI scraping and their work being posted to other websites without their permission. Others resorted to other platforms to get their Dramione or Hollanov fix, such as Tumblr, which reported a 75 percent jump in new sign-ups among users between the ages of 18 and 25, according to data shared with WIRED.

Throughout the 17-day shutdown, AO3 has remained vague about the causes of the security breach. In its statement announcing its return, OTW said that while it has “no reason to believe that the user database was compromised,” it can’t rule out the possibility; the website recommends users change their passwords “as a precaution.” The site is also pairing with a security firm “to help prevent future incidents.”

Though the suggestion prompted some concern on social media, for the most part fans are jubilant about the end of the “AO3 apocalypse,” as some have referred to the shutdown.

“Ao3 returned on a Sunday,” one fan wrote in a tweet that has 1.2 million views. “Just like Jesus.”

Instagram just gave creators one less reason to say "link in bio."

Starting Nov. 16, eligible U.S. creators can now add Amazon affiliate links right to their Reels and feed posts, according to head of Instagram Adam Mosseri, with room for up to 30 products in a Reel and 20 in a feed post.

"A lot of creators make money with affiliate links, but you've mostly had to share them in stories or bio," Mosseri wrote in a post. He added that the feature is "free to add, and we don't take any cut of what you earn."

Creators have long sent followers to a Story, a DM, or their profile to find those links. Now the recommendation and the link can live in the same post. Creators who connect an Amazon Associates account can also paste a regular Amazon product URL and still get credit for qualifying sales. #365. Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it

While we’re used to predictable technology, AI challenges that assumption. Therefore, the goal must be bounded, observable, and controllable AI.

In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.

Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

#362. Paul Barril, French ‘Supergendarme’ Turned Mercenary, Has Died

After years in elite police units, he drew scrutiny from human rights groups for selling arms and providing other services to unsavory governments. He was 80.

Paul Barril’s offer to African dictators was straightforward: Your opponents will be subjected to surveillance and manipulation. Newspapers will be “infiltrated.” Plots against the state will be “neutralized.”

Plenty of heads of state took up the services he offered, including Omar Bongo in Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso in Congo. Other clients went to Paris to do their shopping at his Security Action Store, which offered the latest in bulletproof vests or night-vision goggles, as Mr. Barril recounted in one of his six autobiographies, “The Elysee’s Secret Wars” (1996).

Mr. Barril was often described in the news media as a former French “supergendarme” for his longtime work in elite units. After he left the gendarmerie, or national police, in 1984, he became a security adviser and mercenary provider across the African continent and was implicated by human rights groups in the Rwandan genocide of 1994.

His death, on Oct. 20 at 80 at his home in Antibes, France, was announced by the French interior ministry. He had Parkinson’s disease.

By the time he founded his mercenary-security company, Secrets, a French acronym for Security Equipment Planning and Realization Company, in 1984, Mr. Barril was a well-chronicled public figure.

In the gendarmerie, which in France is under the military, he joined a new military police intervention unit, the GIGN, in 1974. The French news media chronicled Mr. Barril’s reputation as an ultrafit top cop, a military-grade swimmer and diver, a black belt in karate, a parachutist, a hostage liberator and a policeman working inside and outside the law. With the GIGN, he participated in the 1979 operation against Islamist militants who had seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, taking dozens hostage.

#361. Instagram Is Bringing Amazon Affiliate Links Directly to Reels and Posts

Instagram announced a change on Monday that may spell the end for users being nudged to visit a creator’s “link in bio.” At least when they’re promoting products sold on Amazon.

Starting today, creators and businesses can attach multiple Amazon affiliate links to their Instagram content—up to 30 per video or 20 per regular feed post. (Affiliate links let creators earn a commission on any resulting sales.) To participate in this Amazon program, creators must be US-based adults with a professional account that has over 1,000 followers.

Instagram’s parent company, Meta, dropped this shopping-focused change right before the holiday season really kicks off. As creators look to cash in on Amazon's sales, you might expect an avalanche of affiliate posts as you sip hot cocoa and scroll through Reels. But Instagram claims this won’t be the case.

“We don’t expect a sudden influx of shopping content from this launch,” Instagram spokesperson Megan Buckley tells WIRED. “Instagram’s recommendation systems will continue to recommend content based on people’s interests and what we think they’ll enjoy and find valuable. This update makes creators’ product recommendations easier to shop.”

For years, Instagram users could attach a single external link to their bio information. This led to the rise of bundlers like Linktree, where creators could create simple one-page sites with multiple links to content, like shopping recommendations or news articles. In 2023, Instagram expanded the number of links allowed in profiles to five. This most recent update could change how it feels to scroll Instagram, moving more shopping nudges from Amazon storefronts hidden in the bio to direct links on the viral videos.

In an example shared by Meta, a woman recording a Reel leans into her camera as she applies makeup. The caption reads: “My favorite lip tint these days!” Above the creator’s name, a small image tile pops up with the Amazon product. Tap the product and a page opens inside Instagram with the price. Tap one of the listed items, and Instagram will bump you over to the Amazon app or website to complete your purchase.

This change comes as social media shopping habits continue to expand and evolve. TikTok, one of Meta’s primary competitors, has been quite successful in expanding users’ purchasing habits through the app. Around this time last year, an analytics firm estimated that $19 billion worth of products were sold globally through TikTok Shop, putting it at roughly the same size as eBay. Unlike TikTok, however, Instagram will not take a cut of the sales (at least for now). Reddit is also experimenting with how users shop, heading into this holiday season, recently announcing Reddit Reviews, which uses generative AI to summarize user sentiment about products.

For over a decade, Instagram developers have searched for ways to streamline how users spend money through the app. In 2016, WIRED wrote about how the social media app added select commerce links from brands like Warby Parker, a fairly novel attempt at the time to get people to buy stuff through social media. A few years later, the Instagram experience morphed into something like a “digital mall” with in-app checkouts.

This latest attempt moves links from creator bios and places them directly in users' feeds. While this could be a boon for creators, the platform’s implementation could annoy users, who are already inundated with ads online. We’ll see if this change clicks.

#360. The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back

Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

#356. The iPhone Duo Is Getting a Limited Version of Face ID

Apple's most expensive smartphone—the iPhone Duo—lacks one of the company's hallmark features: Face ID. The folding phone is already jam-packed with a hinge and multiple display layers, leaving no room for the TrueDepth sensor required for biometric face authentication. The Duo relies on Touch ID instead.

That's changing now in a software update. On Monday, Apple announced that it's bringing facial recognition to the iPhone Duo as part of the iOS 27.3 developer beta update. But since it can't rely on the tried-and-true Face ID system without those crucial components, it's borrowing the feature from the company's recently launched smart display, the HomeView.

The HomeView personalizes the display content for up to six people in a household, with its camera recognizing people who step in front of it. (It also uses voice data for recognition when someone asks Siri a command.) This “person recognition” technology is protected by the Secure Exclave—different from the Secure Enclave chip that houses Face ID data—a memory-protected space in Apple's A20 Pro processor. As WIRED's Lily Hay Newman writes, it's still not as comprehensive as Face ID, and could be more susceptible to attacks.

At launch, the iPhone Duo relied on Touch ID for biometric authentication.

Rumors abound that Apple is racing to add proper Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo. Still, tight development cycles might mean the feature may not arrive until the third generation in 2028. That also points to limitations in the Duo's new face recognition tech.

You cannot use it to authenticate payments or unlock sensitive content, like your banking app. You'll still need your thumbprint or passcode to approve Apple Wallet purchases. Instead, it's designed to unlock the foldable without tapping a finger on the Touch ID sensor. There is also a time-based limitation. For face recognition to work, it needs a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication within a 45-minute window. This capability is also restricted to the front screen and camera—it doesn't work if the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Also in iOS 27.3, Apple has a new toggle that lets you lock your iPhone Duo when you close it.

Google's newer Pixel folding phones are the only ones on the US market with secure facial authentication, though it's not as effective in the dark as Apple's Face ID. Samsung's facial biometrics on its Galaxy phones aren't strong enough to protect sensitive content and are largely used to unlock the device.

Apple’s willingness to roll out a watered-down version of Face ID is a rare compromise for the company—and shows just how much of a friction point Touch ID has become for Duo owners.

#355. Howard Lutnick Took Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew

Critics say Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his department have shielded Nvidia as concerns have grown over A.I. chip sales to firms like Megaspeed.

Howard Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology to Asia, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales in the region.Credit...Doug Mills/The New York Times

By Ana SwansonTripp MickleMaggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan

Ana Swanson, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported from Washington, and Tripp Mickle from San Francisco.

There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.

Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.

The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.

The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.

The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.

Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

#354. OpenAI launches tool for finding child sexual abuse material

OpenAI announced Monday the release of a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including content generated by artificial intelligence.

The tool is a classifier that looks for visual signs of abuse in images. It then scores images to help human reviewers prioritize which of them warrant attention. OpenAI said its CSAM classifier is the first broadly available tool of its kind to include a specific signal indicating the image may be generated with AI.

This capability is becoming critical as AI-generated CSAM skyrockets.

A new analysis conducted by Childlight — Global Child Safety Institute at the University of Edinburgh found AI-related reports of CSAM increased globally by more than 8,400 percent from 2023 to 2025. Last year, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children received more than 400,000 of these reports. In 2023, that number was roughly 4,700.

"Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online," OpenAI said in its blog post about the announcement.

The company's new tool can be used by organizations required or authorized to detect CSAM, including certain developers that use OpenAI's application programming interface, or API. OpenAI also launched the tool to work with open source detection-and-reporting software called Coop. The software, which is offered by the nonprofit organization ROOST, allows users to both flag and review content and report it to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children.

In addition to launching the classifier, OpenAI also created a model card for it. OpenAI routinely uses model cards to provide detailed information about how its ChatGPT products have been refined and tested.

Camille François, president of ROOST, told Mashable the CSAM classifier model card is the first in its field.

"OpenAI is setting an important precedent for transparency in child safety," François said in an email. "Builders need to know how well detection tools work and where they fall short. Publishing that evidence helps teams build better safeguards and gives the whole field a clearer view of where to focus research."

The model card explains that early testing led to reduced reviewing of false positives. OpenAI estimates that it could flag nearly half as many images while finding roughly the equivalent number of abusive images as the company's existing tool.

If you are a child being sexually exploited online, or you know a child who is being sexually exploited online, or you witnessed exploitation of a child occur online, you can report it to the CyberTipline, which is operated by the National Center for Missing Exploited & Children.

#348. One of France’s Most Popular Athletes Is Running for President

Centrists want alternatives to a matchup between the far right and far left in the 2027 presidential race. Enter Christine Lagarde, a former central banker — and Teddy Riner, a judo star.

When Teddy Riner, a judo champion and one of France’s most popular athletes, announced this week that he would run for president, it was less a game changer than a welcome diversion. For all of his appeal, Mr. Riner, 37, is unlikely to win the race to replace President Emmanuel Macron next spring.

Yet his quixotic candidacy reveals a hard truth about France’s presidential campaign. Five months before voters go to the polls, many are eager, even desperate, for a fresh face to upend a race that looks increasingly as if it’s on a glide path to the election of France’s first far-right government since World War II.

The main far-right candidate, Marine Le Pen, has held a commanding lead over all her rivals for months — a lead that has only been reinforced by weeks of protests, marred by violence, that have shaken France. The most prominent center-right candidate, Édouard Philippe, has faded in the polls as the unrest has sharpened the appeal of far-right calls for law and order and left-wing calls for social justice.

Another beneficiary of the upheaval is a far-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who now appears to be the likeliest candidate to advance into a second round against Ms. Le Pen in France’s two-round system. As things currently stand, French voters would be confronted with a choice between two poles of the political spectrum.

Centrist voters are “afraid of being confronted with a duel between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon,” said Jean-Daniel Lévy, deputy director of Toluna France, a polling firm. These voters, he said, are an “orphan electorate,” lacking an inspiring candidate, and are “still looking for someone.”

Raphaël LLorca, an analyst at the Jean-Jaurès Foundation, a left-leaning research group in Paris, said the search for a white knight showed “the panic of the centrist bloc.” He added, “It is clear that the election is slipping away from them.”

#346. 2023 March Madness: Will UConn or San Diego State triumph in the national championship game that 'means everything?'

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He said going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

“We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher said. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” said Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he said.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

CNN’s Steve Almasy and Issy Ronald contributed to this report.
