#312. Improve your Amazon Kindle experience by doing these simple things

Changing a few settings can make your Kindle feel more book-like.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

As ebook and ereader technologies continue to evolve, the actual process of reading a book on a device has also begun to take on some rather fascinating changes. Though there are always going to be detractors who prefer the act of holding a physical book, products like the Amazon Kindle have done their part in making the hobby more accessible than ever before.

Sometimes, though, you may come to the realization that the sterile, almost inhuman feeling of reading a book on a Kindle can harsh your cozy vibe. It's something that has plagued the digital book market for years, but thanks to a few handy little upgrades and modifications, you can make reading a Kindle book feel like something far more compelling.

The ebook scene is one that's got its fair share of competitors, but if you are reading a lot of digital books, it's likely that you have one of Amazon's range of Kindle models. To help spiff up your days catching up on reading, we've put together a comprehensive look at how you can make that experience even more enjoyable.

If you already have a Kindle, or have plans to get one, you may want to know which models can do certain things from within the ereader itself. For changing how the Kindle looks and operates on its screen, Amazon offers quite a lot of customization that you may have never even messed around with before.

A common complaint about digital books is that they are, in fact, digital books. The actual weight and feeling of reading a book that's in your hands is gone, but if you're willing to part with some cash, you can change that up pretty easily.

They're a bit on the pricier side, but there are so many cases online that can make the Kindle look like a book. There are some genuinely charming and beautiful designs, many of which can help evoke the texts of yesteryear that made you fall in love with books to begin with. A quick Amazon search for "Kindle book cover" will get you started.

When you have a book open on your Kindle, you have a lot of ways to change how each one looks. Nearly all of them will allow you to change the display to fit a book-style criteria, and one of the easiest ways to do that is by changing the font to something that looks more book-like.

With a book open, look for the Aa symbol at the top. This will allow you to open the settings for that book, and by navigating to Font Family in the Font menu, you can change it to something that feels more appropriate. If you want something that is more traditional and less computer-like, a serif font like Baskerville or Palatino will be a great help.

Combining landscape mode with a two-column layout, which you can turn on by pressing Aa and navigating to Orientation in the Layout tab, can also help make the Kindle feel more like a book with two pages.

Another way to make the layout of each book feel more natural is to go into settings and change the margins and text weights. By widening the margins, therefore narrowing the way your eyes scan each block of text, you can get your Kindle display to have extra space around the edges of the text in the same way a book does. If you combine this with increasing the weight of the text, essentially giving it a bolder appearance by going into the Font menu, it helps make each passage look more print-like.

If you have a long history of reading physical books, reading a Kindle may be difficult to get used to at first. One of the reasons it feels less like an actual book is the bright, digital screen that you're reading it on as opposed to paper. By adjusting the brightness and display output, you can dial in something more nostalgic.

With a book open, tap the top of the screen, and you'll be given access to the Kindle's Quick Actions menu. Crushing the brightness a bit and then turning the warmth up helps create something that feels a lot closer to a physical book.

Some of you may not be aware of this, but you can adjust how the book is actually consumed minute to minute by turning on page-turn animations, which help to get you closer to the feel of reading an actual book. These aren't supported on every single Kindle, mostly being on Amazon's Colorsoft, Paperwhite and Scribe, as well as mobile versions.

This creates a gentle transition as you tap or swipe between pages. While it doesn't necessarily recreate the genuine, tactile feel of turning a page, it does help to keep the illusion of reading a book at the forefront of your brain. It can really let you sink into whatever you're reading.

#311. SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch

STARBASE, Texas—The black-and-silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontally until the last moment, when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.

Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about 1 foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.

This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.

Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power and be captured by the tower.

It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.

Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

The shuttles were engineering marvels. But during the return to Earth they acted as gliders, not igniting their engines. And their heat shields were delicate flowers, requiring painstaking refurbishment after each flight. At the outset of the shuttle program, the space agency contemplated sending dozens of humans into space at a time, and carrying cargo at a cost as low of $25 per pound.

Reality never matched these rosy projections. The crew space capped out at seven astronauts, and the cost-per-pound was closer to $25,000. Each orbiter cost an extraordinary amount of money to build; NASA only ever built five that went to space.

SpaceX has five Starships in an advanced state of development at Starbase today; and its factory houses the components for a dozen more. The company can currently manufacture a Starship upper stage in its South Texas Starfactory every three weeks. The factory was sized to produce a ship every three days. When SpaceX founder Elon Musk discussed these build targets in an interview five years ago, he sounded mad. But he no longer does.

The Space Shuttle was nearly a fully reusable space launch system, but it fell far short of low-cost rapid launch. Over 30 years the vehicle made 135 flights. Within a few years SpaceX aims to fly 135 times a year, then thousands of times.

Such was the significance of Saturday. SpaceX aspires to fundamentally change the relationship between humanity and the heavens. The first step is to get the entire rocket back. SpaceX has now returned both elements of a Starship rocket safely to its launch tower. It will take time to reach a high rate of success with such landings, but Saturday’s safe return offered a proof of concept.

The landings will come with increasing frequency; and so will the launches. Over time SpaceX will perfect the heat shield that is likely to be the most difficult aspect of rapid reuse. And eventually, as difficult as it may be to believe, what we experienced with amazement this weekend will become routine. One day, we will take this all for granted.

Google is making these Ask Maps updates available on Android and iOS starting today. The list search and travel itinerary features can be used anywhere that Ask Maps is up and running. #309. Chelsea searches for new manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s plan for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected new signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

#307. How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause

COVID-19 lockdowns cut global fire activity by 12.3 percent.

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.

Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.

An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.

Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”

The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.

In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.

The results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.

Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.

The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.

Wang said, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”

In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.

There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.

One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.

Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.

When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.

This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.

Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.

Wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.

Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

Cell Reports Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.crsus.2026.100860

#306. Europe Agrees on a Team to Represent It in Talks With Russia

After coveting a seat in the Ukraine war discussions, Europe is poised to get one. The continent wants to fill it with a six-member team.

Reporting from Dublin, where European leaders are meeting, and from an airfield near the city where Americans and Ukrainians debriefed on Thursday night.

European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. They learned this week that they would get one, and simply needed to decide which official should sit in that chair.

European Union leaders concluded in Dublin on Friday that they will tap a group of major nations — Britain, France, Germany, Poland, and Italy — along with a representative from the E.U’s leadership arms, the European Council and European Commission.

In some ways, the choice of a crowd plays into jibes Americans have made about the continent’s indecisiveness: “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said earlier this week.

Europe’s failure to pick one negotiator leaves open the possibility that its fragmentation will diminish its influence. Even so, Europeans have underscored that they are a democracy of many nations and that many voices must be represented.

“We decide on who represents us, and that is what we have done today,” said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission.

“We need to work as a team,” António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, said at a news conference on Friday, noting that America itself has two envoys.

#305. Which Google Pixel phone is most similar to the Galaxy S26+?

Google Pixel is considered the cleanest Android experience, but which model holds up against the Samsung Galaxy S26+?

On paper, Samsung's Galaxy S26 and Google's Pixel 11 family of smartphones look surprisingly alike. You get three models to choose from on either side of the divide, but pit the two companies' offerings head-to-head and you'll find that the comparison isn't as straightforward.

For instance, the Galaxy S26+ specifically sits in the middle of Samsung's flagship lineup. However, you'll need to step up to Google's top-of-the-line Pixel 11 Pro XL for a direct equivalent. The Pixel 11 Pro also comes close to offering the same experience, but it makes a few tradeoffs while undercutting the Galaxy S26+ on price by a small margin.

With that in mind, here's how the Pixel 11 series stacks up against the Galaxy S26+, the middle child of Samsung's flagship smartphone lineup. Let's start with the Pixel 11 Pro, which seems like a natural competitor to the Galaxy S26+ as they each occupy the middle slot in Google and Samsung's flagship portfolios, respectively. Look a bit closer, though, and you'll find some fairly significant differences between them.

Samsung's Galaxy S26+ is a fairly large smartphone — it packs a 6.7-inch display that's only 0.2 inches smaller than the S26 Ultra. The Pixel 11 Pro, meanwhile, is quite compact by modern smartphone standards as we found out in our review. It has a 6.3-inch display, which is exactly the same as the base Galaxy S26.

If you don't mind the screen size difference, though, the Pixel 11 Pro is nearly an even match for the Galaxy S26+ in many other ways. In fact, Google's Pro phone offers a brighter display and more capable set of cameras. One major caveat is that the Galaxy S26 series enjoys a healthy lead in terms of raw performance. Google's Tensor G6 is primarily designed to support AI workloads, while the Galaxy S26's Snapdragon Elite Gen 5 — quoted as the "world's faster mobile system-on-a-chip" at launch by manufacturer Qualcomm — delivers considerably more processing and graphics horsepower (as does its international Exynos 2600 chip).

Still, the Pixel 11's Tensor G6 can handle day-to-day tasks and even multitasking just fine. The Galaxy S26+ simply pulls ahead in gaming, video editing and other resource-intensive applications. But on the plus side, the Pixel 11 Pro's $1,099 price tag undercuts the Galaxy S26+'s $1,199 MSRP.

If you find the Pixel 11 Pro too small, Google's larger Pro XL model is a much closer match to the Galaxy S26+. Its 6.8-inch display is a touch larger than the 6.7-inch panel found on Samsung's middleweight flagship. Google also equips the Pixel 11 Pro with superior camera hardware, offering a 50MP primary lens, 48MP ultrawide and 48MP telephoto with 5x optical zoom. The Galaxy S26+ has a 50MP main camera but only a 12MP ultrawide and 10MP telephoto with 3x optical zoom. Samsung reserves its best optical sensors for the top-of-the-line Galaxy S26 Ultra.

At $1,299, the Pixel 11 Pro XL is $100 more than the Galaxy S26+'s $1,199 MSRP. Because Samsung's flagship line has been on the market longer, you're more likely to score a discount on the Galaxy S26+. You'll also notice a major difference in hand: the largest Pixel weighs a hefty 8 ounces (226 grams) compared to the 6.7-ounce (190-gram) Galaxy S26+. It's easy to notice the difference when holding the phones in the real world. The Pixel 11 Pro XL feels reassuringly hefty, but that feeling can eventually turn to fatigue during extended use.

#304. California sues OpenAI after that Hugging Face rogue hacking incident

State AG Rob Bonta has accused the company of making AI agents “without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect” users.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has filed a sweeping lawsuit against OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. Bonta has accused the entity of developing AI models "without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public."

The suit centers on the now famous Hugging Face incident, in which dozens of AI agents created by OpenAI reportedly went rogue and hacked computer systems at another company. The organization says its agents hacked Hugging Face on their own after escaping confinement and has since called for "stronger safeguards and defensive tools."

We're suing OpenAI for its testing and development of dangerous AI models without adequate safeguards.

In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law.https://t.co/SKCO15uzHx pic.twitter.com/IZCAnVm2ju

— Rob Bonta (@AGRobBonta) November 16, 2026

Bonta, however, alleges the attack was "entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI's choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight." It is worth noting that we don't even know exactly which models were involved in the hack. OpenAI just says it was a combination that included GPT-5.6 but also an "even more capable pre-release model."

The AG's office has accused the ChatGPT maker of creating a "public nuisance" by failing to secure the testing of its models. Bonta went on to allege that this represents a violation of California's Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits businesses in the state from engaging in illegal or fraudulent practices.

"The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability," he said in a statement. "In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law."

OpenAI has yet to comment on the suit. It wrote in a blog post back in August that "without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls" and "take dangerous actions that no human directed."

California's suit looks to mandate some of those proper safeguards, as it would force OpenAI to implement monitoring systems and secure testing environments. Bonta is seeking civil penalties of $2,500 per violation.

#302. Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors

This was the first total mission failure in United Launch Alliance’s 20-year history.

United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.

The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.

Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents triggered monthslong reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.

Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).

In a statement, ULA said the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”

“ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”

Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible,” ULA said.

“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.”

The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially said the anomaly occurred.

Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage issue was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.

Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’ space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.

Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.

A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, showed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.

ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The company then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.

First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the company’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.

The Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the company has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.

Amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers.

Previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently announced it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.

“There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon said in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

Amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’ Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan launches in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that company’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have launched so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.

Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.

What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.

That would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’ chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.

It’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.

Vulcan’s earlier delays forced Space Force officials to move six national security launches from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.

Expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.

But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s company is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and new orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed plans yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.

Amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 launches it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s New Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.

NASA’s lunar program has another important link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently announced it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.

“Appreciate you quickly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”

#300. Microsoft’s Global Outage and Fixes: What We Know

Disruptions to the company’s email, messaging and other products lasted about 36 hours, hampering companies and services around the world.

Microsoft said early Saturday that it had fully restored its services after a global outage disrupted them for a day and a half, hampering communications and work at schools, government agencies and offices around the world.

The problems began on Thursday and cascaded around the world. The company, based in Redmond, Wash., gradually restored service through Friday until declaring an end to one of its most extensive outages of recent times in an update on Saturday around 1 a.m. Eastern time.

Outages started disrupting Microsoft tools and apps around noon Eastern time on Thursday and quickly spread to more than 70 countries and territories, affecting millions of users, according to Downdetector, an outage-tracking site.

Some of Microsoft’s most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot, stopped working.

Microsoft said in a statement on Friday that “for now, we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” It added that the problem was “a technical issue not related to cyber or A.I.” agents.

The company said it had no indication that a Federal Aviation Administration ground stop issued late Friday afternoon, which has affected air travel nationwide, was related to the outage.

#299. Delivery drones are coming. For some with PTSD, that's a terrifying prospect.

For those who have lived under armed drones, the sound overhead can be distressing.

In August, Amazon announced plans to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.” Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace.

For many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous. For others, though, their growing use could be a nightmare. As the instant delivery industry clears the last FAA hurdles to rapid deliveries beyond an operator’s line of sight, an increasing number of people worldwide are living with post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders triggered by drones.

The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia.” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media.

Combined with broader anxiety about surveillance technologies, artificial intelligence, and things generally falling from the sky, the resulting hypervigilance could result in some unintended deliveries from those Prime Air flying robots.

Drones have been a part of the battlefield in some form since the late 1980s, when the Israeli Defense Forces began using them. From the beginning, they have had a psychological impact on both those in the sights of drone operators and the operators themselves.

The first military use of drones was for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. I witnessed the development of naval drone operations aboard USS Iowa in 1986 and 1987, and for many on the ship at the time, the drones were a curiosity—or, at worst, an annoyance. Our crews spent hours standing by a boat, ready to retrieve crashed drones from the water. But we were helping develop a capability that would eventually lead to Iraqi troops surrendering to the USS Wisconsin‘s drone during the Gulf War. Back then, drones were merely heralds of destruction, acting as forward observers for the Air Force ordnance fired or launched from elsewhere.

Iraqi troops on Faylaka Island associated the Pioneer RPV with the bombardment they had just experienced from the USS Missouri. When the Wisconsin’s drone flew in to assess the damage, their morale was broken.

Over southern Lebanon, the same kinds of drones were part of what amounted, for some residents, to sonic psychological warfare—the hum of lawnmower-like engines overhead was a reminder of constant surveillance and the ever-present threat of artillery or air strikes. The resulting anxiety intensified as drones began carrying their own weapons and “loitering munitions,” one-way drones designed to fly into targets and explode.

Israel’s continued fight against Hezbollah in Lebanon, along with the US wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, accelerated the evolution of drone warfare and expanded the population experiencing its psychological effects. A Stanford Law study in 2012 of the impact of US drones in Pakistan (PDF) highlighted how drones were destroying the fabric of communities in northwest Pakistan:

Drones hover twenty-four hours a day over communities in northwest Pakistan, striking homes, vehicles, and public spaces without warning. Their presence terrorizes men, women, and children, giving rise to anxiety and psychological trauma among civilian communities. Those living under drones have to face the constant worry that a deadly strike may be fired at any moment and the knowledge that they are powerless to protect themselves.

That experience has been repeated and amplified in current conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Ukraine. A team of US and Ukrainian psychiatrists has reported that Ukrainian military personnel and civilians who have experienced a drone attack, particularly those injured in one, “are at heightened risk for developing persistent psychological symptoms, a vulnerability intensified by the ongoing threat of repeated attacks.”

Those symptoms—a “unique hypervigilance behavior with corresponding hyperarousal and avoidance behaviors”—are now referred to by some Ukrainian doctors as “dronophobia.”

“The distinct hum of an approaching drone, often likened to the swarming of hornets, has itself become a psychological weapon,” noted the team led by Dr. Joseph L. Bonvie of Massachusetts General Hospital. “The escalating pitch as a drone draws near elicits fear and helplessness even before an attack.”

Similar symptoms have been reported in women and children in Gaza, where Israeli drone strikes have been persistent. In consultations with 19 patients in Gaza, “all patients reported an intense phobic reaction to the acoustic signature of drones (the ‘zannana’), associated with imminent bombing and death, manifesting as full-blown panic attacks,” wrote Dr. Mohammad Abu Slaih, a Jordanian psychiatrist, in an article for European Psychiatry. “Three children developed a specific fear of looking at the sky. “

The Iranian drone attacks on Gulf states, while hardly comparable to what Gaza has endured, have had a broad impact on civilians in the United Arab Emirates and other countries in the region, disrupting sleep, causing fatigue, and fueling anticipatory anxiety as people wait for the next drone to strike.

That anxiety is common across populations exposed to drone warfare. The US Army Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC) has compared drones’ potential to induce PTSD to the “shell shock” of World War I and the “battle fatigue” of World War II, noting that the “fear and stress from (the sound of) near-persistent drone presence creates anticipatory anxiety… Fears can persist beyond the drone’s presence, enhancing a soldier’s anxiety even when out of harm’s way.”

The use of drone video by both Russia and Ukraine as a psychological warfare tool extends the impact of drones beyond those who experience attacks firsthand. Footage of attacks on individual soldiers has been posted on social media to spread anxiety among opposing forces, sometimes going viral and exposing thousands of other people to the attacks. Ukrainian military units often publish first-person-view videos of drones chasing down Russian soldiers, complete with horror-film-styled soundtracks.

According to Neda Gould, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, that aspect sets drone-induced PTSD apart from other types of the disorder. In an interview with Psychiatry Online, Gould said social media could amplify trauma because “not only does the soldier have to grapple with the PTSD-related consequences of the attack itself, but they may also relive the experience in a way that is completely out of their control,” especially when social media comments express support for the attacks.

The US military has grappled with drone-induced PTSD and other mental health symptoms over the past 15 years. The first signs of stress for American troops, however, came from drone operators themselves.

In 2014, a team of researchers led by a US Air Force psychologist found that 4.3 percent of Air Force drone operators displayed “a pattern of symptoms of moderate to extreme level of severity” associated with PTSD. More recent studies have found that drone operators are just as likely to experience PTSD symptoms as members of aircrews deployed to war zones. Differences in how crews operate between manned combat aircraft and unmanned systems crews may even put drone operators at greater risk of psychological impact.

The dual psychological impact of drone warfare was aptly demonstrated by Killbox, a video artwork and “game” that presents two perspectives: those of a drone operator and a child on the ground. Playing it leaves many people deeply saddened, offering a glimpse of the moral injury some drone operators have experienced after their missions.

US troops are no longer just the ones behind the screens, however. Beginning with operations against ISIS, US troops have faced increasingly sophisticated drone warfare, starting with grenades dropped by ISIS-operated consumer quadcopter drones in 2017. Since then, Iranian-built drones, some based on reverse-engineered technology from downed US drones, have been used against US troops and ships by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in Yemen and Iraq. Among these is the Shahed, a long-range attack drone that Iran has sold in large numbers to Russia for its war on Ukraine.

The US Army TRADOC report also recognized that the psychological effects of drone attacks can reach further than those wounded in attacks, and even beyond the units that encounter them, saying:

Drones amplify the uncertainties of war because rear areas are less secure as long-range drones extend danger zones beyond that of artillery and rockets. The feeling of nowhere being safe exacerbates anxiety even when drones are not present.

While little public data is available on drone-induced PTSD among US veterans, evidence suggests that drones could also affect people with PTSD stemming from other kinds of trauma. The sound of a drone, its shadow, a glimpse of one in peripheral vision, or other stimuli from drones could trigger hypervigilance because of their unexpectedness, their similarity to other triggering stimuli, or a range of other factors.

Even for those who have not experienced drone attacks, the presence of an uncrewed aircraft can cause anxiety. Drones purportedly operated by the Department of Homeland Security in Minneapolis earlier this year appeared to be used not just for surveillance of targets of Immigration and Customs Enforcement but also to intimidate individuals who had been tracking ICE activity.

The expanding use of drones by law enforcement organizations in the US as part of “drone first responder” programs has exposed an increasing number of Americans to drone surveillance, with over 1,000 agencies applying for FAA waivers for drone operations as of February 2026, based on data from the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Combined with news reports about drone attacks and foreign governments’ use of drones, the disquiet of drone propeller noises and blinking lights in the sky has already created a War of the Worlds level of dronophobia.

Over the past two years, several drone incidents have been linked, or suspected of being linked, to state-actor espionage, with a surge in reports in November and December of 2024. Three occurred in Southern California, including a drone flyover of Vandenberg Air Force Base as a National Reconnaissance Office payload was being loaded ont0 a SpaceX rocket. A Chinese national was charged in the case and arrested while attempting to leave the country. Other cases in the US were officially downplayed as posing no security threat.

In November 2024, incidents in the UK centered on multiple air bases used by the US, including incursions near RAF Fairford, the base recently allegedly targeted in a plot that the British government attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Similar incursions occurred in Germany.

Around the same time, a rash of civilian “drone sightings” across the US emerged, particularly in New Jersey. Anxiety grew further after a Republican New Jersey congressman claimed there was an “Iranian drone mothership.” Segments of the population were ready to shoot down drones themselves.

Many of these sightings turned out to be crewed aircraft or helicopters, toy drones, or, in very few cases, authorized commercial drone flights. Former Maryland Governor Larry Hogan even reported seeing dozens of large drones above his house, only for others to quickly point out that the objects were actually the constellation Orion.

PTSD is a treatable condition, and coping strategies can help people manage triggers. But severe PTSD can be extremely debilitating, and research into the effects of drones on PTSD remains limited. It’s still unclear how well survivors of drone attacks will be able to process the fears and traumatic memories associated with drones, especially if the aircraft become a pervasive part of daily life.

I, for one, won’t be placing any Prime Air orders anytime soon.

#298. Every Xbox console generation sorted by release date

Celebrate 25 years of Xbox with a trip down memory lane.

Since taking a crack at gaming in 2001, Microsoft has rolled out nine distinct Xbox variations across four generations (not including different SKUs like the Xbox 360 Arcade). From the jump, the line has introduced new ideas that (literally) changed the game, like revolutionizing online console gaming, introducing achievements and launching a subscription-based game library with Xbox Game Pass.

With it being 25 years since the first console and its little shooter game about aliens hit shelves, it's a great chance to take a trip down memory lane. While details about the next Xbox are still up in the air, now's the time to reminisce. Let's start at the top, from the days of the Duke controller to "everything is an Xbox."

In 2001, the original $300 Xbox went toe-to-toe with Sony and Nintendo, who had released the PS2 and GameCube in the US within a 13 month-period. The sales affirm that the PS2 was by far this generation's most popular console — and the best-selling console of all time, in fact. But Microsoft deserves tons of credit for the high standard it set for online gaming with Xbox Live, which launched in late 2002.

The Xbox 360 launched in 2005 in two configurations. The $400 Premium had a wireless controller and a detachable 20GB hard drive pre-loaded with a few goodies. Meanwhile, the $300 Core had a wired controller and no hard drive, forcing owners to buy one separately or use a memory card for save data.

After the PlayStation 3 and Wii came out in 2006, Microsoft upped the ante in 2007 with the pictured Elite configuration. It featured a matte black finish, a 120GB hard drive and, arguably most important of all, an HDMI port.

Then in 2010, Microsoft released the 360 Slim, tackling the original's infamous overheating problem that often led to the Red Ring of Death. This revamped model had a whole new cooling system and up to 320GB of storage. Ultimately, Microsoft ushered this famed generation out with the 360 E in June 2013, introducing a sleeker design just months before the Xbox One arrived.

Even with the Red Ring, Microsoft's second-gen console remains its best-selling ever, with at least 84 million units sold. This generation rolled out features like achievements and Gamerscore, rewarding progress and often giving a reason to revisit games. Speaking of which, the Xbox 360's now-iconic exclusive games may be coming to PC, giving us a chance to replay hits like Halo 3, Fable II, Gears of War and Forza Motorsport 2.

Although the Wii is often viewed as the biggest reason for motion-control gaming going mainstream, Microsoft's Kinect tried taking the idea in a new direction in 2010. It tracked the player's whole body with a camera, rather than a sensor bar only tracking a remote. While it was optional to start, Microsoft had different plans when the next generation arrived.

Microsoft gambled out of the gate when it revealed the Xbox One in summer 2013, planning to bundle the $499 console with a Kinect 2.0 and forcing players to keep the motion camera plugged in. Before the console hit shelves in November, the company reversed this and asserted that Kinect wouldn't be necessary, to the delight of many. Come 2014, the company dropped the Xbox One's price to $400 and stopped bundling the two.

The console also answered a long-running taunt from PS3 owners with its built-in Blu-ray player. It also came with a 500GB hard drive and a slightly redesigned controller with new thumbsticks, impulse triggers and other upgrades.

Over the generation, the Xbox One got a few hardware upgrades. The $399 Xbox One S arrived in 2016 with no dedicated Kinect port. Failed accessories aside, this iteration notably brought 4K support to the table, now featuring a 4K Blu-ray player, 4K streaming capabilities and 1080p upscaling. Plus, it was 40 percent smaller than the huge original model.

Then in 2017, the $499 Xbox One X became Microsoft's first console to deliver native 4K gameplay, with HDR support to match. To make the most of this, Microsoft rolled out Xbox One X Enhanced versions of many titles, offering higher resolutions and frame rates. But since not every re-released game took full advantage, native 4K support varied by title.

The Xbox Series X was unveiled in 2019, a year before hitting shelves for the 2020 holiday season at $500. Self-positioned as Microsoft's fastest and most powerful console to date, it promised ultra-low latency and native 4K gaming that could max out at 120FPS, as well as eventual support for 8K capabilities (though 8K is essentially dead now).

These days, after several price increases, the Series S starts at $500 for the 512GB system, while the Series X is $750 for the digital 1TB console or $800 with a disc drive. And serving as a perfect bookend to this timeline, Microsoft celebrated the OG console's 25th anniversary this year with a translucent green Series X, an homage to the iconic model from 2001.

#297. Emma Heming Willis shares family photos as daughter Mabel turns 11

Bruce Willis’ wife, Emma Heming Willis, has celebrated their elder daughter’s birthday with a trip down memory lane.

Mabel Willis turned 11 on Sunday, and her proud mom marked the occasion by sharing a montage of family photos and videos taken over the years, set to the song “Pictures Of You” by The Cure.

“Happy 11th Birthday Mabel Ray!” Heming Willis wrote in the caption.

Emma Heming Willis speaks out about finding community as a caregiver: 'This journey can feel very dark'

“Your energy is infectious,” she continued, praising her little girl for the way she “can light a whole room with your smile and warmth.”

“How you love and care for your family and friends is beautiful to witness. Keep shining my love and always remember to #liveitup,” Heming Willis added.

Heming Willis and Willis married in 2009. Along with Mabel, the couple also have an 8-year-old daughter, Evelyn. Willis also has daughters Rumer, Scout and Tallulah with his ex-wife, Demi Moore.

Willis is clearly a doting dad. One picture in Heming Willis’ montage shows the “Die Hard” star holding baby Mabel while planting a kiss on her forehead, while a more recent image shows a beaming Willis hanging out in nature with his preteen.

Bruce Willis sings with his family in birthday tribute video from ex Demi Moore

Heming Willis penned an equally heartfelt tribute last month when her husband celebrated his 68th birthday. Sharing a video montage on Instagram, she referred to the actor as “pure love.”

In February, Willis’ family announced that his speaking disorder, aphasia, had progressed into a form of dementia called frontotemporal dementia, or FTD.

“Today there are no treatments for the disease, a reality that we hope can change in the years ahead,” they said in an update shared online. “As Bruce’s condition advances, we hope that any media attention can be focused on shining a light on this disease that needs far more awareness and research.”

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, FTD refers to “a group of disorders caused by progressive nerve cell loss in the brain’s frontal lobes (the areas behind your forehead) or its temporal lobes.” These areas of the brain are generally associated with personality, behavior and language.

#295. The iPhone Duo gets face unlock with the latest iOS 27 beta.

You won't need to wait for TouchID on your $2,000 foldable.

The lack of Face ID is one of the main complaints users have had about the iPhone Duo. And while rumors suggest that the company might add a TrueDepth camera to the second generation of its foldable phone next year, it seems that Apple has a more immediate solution to address these complaints. The second beta of iOS 27.3, released to developers on Monday, adds a new option to unlock the iPhone Duo with facial recognition using its front-facing camera.

The feature is called "Unlock with Front Camera" and can be enabled in the Touch ID & Passcode settings in the Settings app. Engadget confirmed that the feature works on an iPhone Duo running the beta — but how it works is quite intriguing. Unlike most modern iPhones, the Duo lacks a TrueDepth camera with the depth sensors that Face ID uses to map a face in 3D. Instead, it has regular cameras on both the outer and inner screens, which is likely the main reason it relies on Touch ID for unlocking.

And the new feature in iOS 27.3 beta makes this very clear — the setup screen warns users that the feature "provides convenience" but "isn't as secure as Touch ID or Face ID." It's still too early to tell, but Engadget's tests show that the feature works reasonably well. It unlocks faster than Touch ID and wasn't fooled when a photo of the user's face was pointed at the camera. It also seems to work in certain low-light conditions, though not when it's completely dark.

Of course, Apple has set some limits to ensure that malicious people don't take advantage of the new feature to tamper with others' iPhones without their consent. It only works to bypass the Lock Screen, and you can't unlock apps, view your passwords or use Apple Pay with your face — Touch ID is still required for more sensitive actions. Not using your phone for more than 45 minutes also temporarily disables Unlock with Front Camera. The feature doesn't work using the iPhone Duo's inner display either, but that's most likely because the under-display camera has a very low resolution.

The approach is very similar to what Apple did with the recently announced HomeView. It also lacks Face ID and relies on a simpler form of facial recognition to identify who is using the device in order to display personal content. It seems that Apple has now brought the same system to the iPhone Duo. In our review, we found the Duo's Touch ID accurate but a bit slower to unlock than expected. The same beta also adds a setting to lock the Duo when it's closed, instead of moving content to the outer display.

Apple hasn't said when iOS 27.3 will be released to the public, but the update is likely to be rolled out sometime mid-December. For now, only developers and beta testers have access to it.
